speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: COMMITTEE NEXT SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house 1 would like to say a few words in respect of one portion of the legislative program, and in particular to answer the question asked a few days ago by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).
This has been a long and, I think, very productive session. There have been more committees sitting than was the case at any time during the years I have been here. I think it would be generally admitted by members in all parts of the house that the work done by those committees has been comprehensive and helpful. The membership of the various committees have been most diligent in the discharge of their responsibilities.
I am not one of those who through the years have advocated the extension of the committee system, but I do feel, while maintaining to the strictest degree our parliamentary system and in no way adopting the system in effect in the United States of America, which meets the needs of that country, this session has shown the benefits that flow from the mobilization of the help of private members everywhere in the house.
I say that as a preface to my remarks in respect of the bill of rights. I am in no way changed in my view as to the necessity of a bill of rights being passed by parliament, and the experience in government in no way has lessened my feelings as to the necessity of such a bill.
As hon. members know, a draft bill was introduced in the concluding days of the last session with a view to assuring that the fullest possible representations might be made by interested bodies, groups and individuals. In that respect there have been many such representations made by private individuals as well as by institutions such as civil rights organizations in various parts of the country and the Canadian Bar Association.
I believe it is generally accepted by hon. members that when the bill of rights finally
passes it shall be as comprehensive and allinclusive as the constitution will permit. Representations and suggestions are being received even now; and while I expressed the view some months ago that there was no necessity, as I saw it then, for a committee of both houses to consider the matter fully in so far as the terms of the suggested bill are concerned, in the light of representations made since I have altered my viewpoint, as I hope I always will when reason demands a change.
I have come to the conclusion that it would be well to have the draft bill of rights submitted to a joint committee of both houses, that committee to consider no other question than the terminology of the bill. As I see it, the question as to the need of a bill of rights would not be a subject for consideration by the committee. Such a committee would provide the fullest possible opportunity for further discussion and consideration, to the end that when the bill is enacted this historic step in the maintenance and preservation of freedom under law will be the most significant that parliament can attain through^ joint counsel and consideration.
In saying that I want to make clear that from the suggestion I have to offer to postpone the introduction of the bill of rights until the beginning of the next session, no one is to take that postponement as any indication of less allegiance on the part of the government and myself to the paramount need of this legislation being passed. Therefore under the circumstances I am going to suggest that the bill of rights already drafted be brought up at the next session at the earhest possible date, and that a joint committee for the purposes I have mentioned be then set up. Even though my views changed during the progress of the present session as to the benefits that might flow from the setting up of such a committee, I realized that with the number of committees that were sitting it would be next to impossible at this session to set up still another committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during consideration of my department's estimates on July 9 the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked two questions, and seeing that we were both in a co-operative mood that night I promised to provide an answer before the end of the session.
His first request was for an estimate of the increased expenditures on general procurement resulting from the establishment of Camp Gagetown. I have now obtained figures for all purchases made in the Atlantic provinces during the fiscal years 1957-58 and 1958-59 which are known to have been destined for Camp Gagetown. For 1957-58 the total was $3,046,479 and for 1958-59, $3,504,354. I have here a table showing the breakdown of these figures by categories, which the hon. member might wish to have incorporated in the record. These figures do not include the value of supplies such as tinned food or clothing and footwear which may have been purchased in the Atlantic provinces for delivery to depots in central Canada and subsequently issued to the camp, since these are not readily identifiable. On the other hand, the figures do include local purchases made directly by the army units stationed at Camp Gagetown.
As the hon. member will notice, the increase from 1957-58 to 1958-59 was slightly less than $500,000, which is only about 7 per cent of the total increase in our purchasing in the Atlantic provinces, as I reported on June 3 and July 9. The ration strength of the camp was, in fact, lower in 1958-59 than in 1957-58. Consequently, although it may be true, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggested, that the establishment of the camp had a stimulating effect on the economy of the area, this does not account for any of the increase in our purchases within the Atlantic provinces in 1958-59.
The other question was what proportion of the expenditures for the Atlantic provinces in the last fiscal year was spent in the province of Newfoundland. The answer to this is 4.1 per cent.
I request permission to have this table printed in Hansard.

It has been a year which certainly will always be remembered, I am sure, by the corporation, and I do not think there is any real purpose that can be served by my discussing the matter at this time. However, there is a statement I do want to make with respect to the C.B.C. and broadcasting which I think should be given to the committee before detailed consideration is given to the estimates.
Hon. members will recall that the previous government in December, 1952 laid down a policy of permitting only one television station in each area, except where there was to be one each in the French and the English languages. This policy was apparently intended to assist in developing and conserving commercial revenue, and also to support an industry which was very expensive and which at that time, at any rate, was in an experimental stage. That policy was criticized by members of the Conservative party then in opposition, and it was criticized as having a monopolistic tendency.
Since the present government took office it has carefully re-examined the situation with a view to changing the previous policy to one of competition and greater freedom. First it was necessary, of course, to establish the board of broadcast governors as an independent regulatory body. This has now been done. It was necessary to assess the general position of both the C.B.C. and private broadcasters in the light of present circumstances and in the light of the whole review made by the royal commission, which reported in 1957. It may be recalled that that commission recommended the abandonment -I want to emphasize this-of the old single station policy and the licensing of competing stations, subject to suitable conditions. In addition, the commission warned of certain problems and difficulties which will no doubt be in the minds of any who seek licences to establish new stations, as well as those who grant such licences.
The establishment of new competing stations in the larger centres of population will no doubt affect the commercial revenues of those now operating there and will, of course, affect particularly perhaps the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation revenues. We are all very conscious of the problems in the financing of the C.B.C. and the difficulties
[Mr. Nowlan.I

it faces in obtaining commercial revenues. On the other hand we believe competition will be of benefit to the consumers of television services, that is to the Canadian people who pay for the services one way or another. We believe also that it will be a spur to improve the efficiency of both private and public operators.
In that connection I might interpolate in my prepared statement and venture to suggest that there has been a great deal of criticism of the C.B.C. for carrying on a certain type of program service. There are those, of course, who think this type of program should be dropped and that type of program should be dropped, but I suggest to this committee that as long as the government maintains the single station policy, then I would think it is almost essential that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has to carry out this broad basis of programming because no other facilities provide them. Once you do get competing services it is possible-and I emphasize "possible"-that the C.B.C. will be in a position to deal with the new problems which arise.
The government has consequently decided that as from September 15, 1959 it will be prepared to consider applications for additional television broadcasting stations in areas already provided with television service. These applications should be made to the Department of Transport in the normal way for checking all their technical features under the Radio Act. They will then be passed to the board of broadcast governors for hearing and decision under the Broadcasting Act. They will finally require, of course, the approval of the government in accordance with that act. Under the policy I am now announcing the government will now be prepared to give that approval if all those previous requisite conditions are met.
It may well be that the size of the market to be served will not justify additional stations in many of the areas already served, and where people are hopeful of obtaining additional licences. This is a matter which the board of broadcast governors no doubt will wish to take carefully into account in considering the proposals which may be put before it. Nevertheless, as time goes on it may be assumed that more and more areas in Canada will justify a second station.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that is all I wish to say at the moment. I know there will be many queries and comments and I shall be prepared to deal with those later, of course.

consideration of C.B.C. matters, because even at this stage of the session-and I wish it could have been earlier-some attention must be given to this very important matter. We discuss the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and broadcasting in Canada at a time of great anxiety about the future of a national broadcasting system in this country, an anxiety the responsibility for which, I suggest, should be shared between the government and the C.B.C. itself.
That principle I have mentioned, one national broadcasting system with its public and private sectors, is basic to our approach to this whole matter. I think it is also the approach of the minister, and anything I may say in criticism of recent policies should not be interpreted as suggesting that I do not have confidence in the minister's approach to what I consider to be basic, as I have said, to the problem of broadcasting in Canada. I think we on this side appreciate his views and the way he has tried to carry them out in this fundamental matter.
We think it essential, Mr. Chairman, that the publicly owned and operated sector of this national system, which is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, should be free from every form of unjustifiable influence or pressure, including, indeed, special pressure from government. To achieve the purpose I have mentioned of establishing a strong and independent national broadcasting system, as independent as such a system can be, subject always to parliamentary control of general policy-because I do not suggest for a minute that independence should go as far as to exclude parliamentary control-the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as the Fowler commission pointed out a few years ago, must have reasonable financial security, some certainty of at least a basic income over a longer time than the period of one year. It must also display administrative efficiency, and that in its turn implies maximum freedom from political pressures. The Fowler commission also stressed that point.
So far as the first matter is concerned, finance, in other days the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation had certain revenues assured by statute though, of course, especially in recent years, they were supplemented by parliamentary votes. That is no longer the case. The minister and the committee will recall that the Fowler commission was appointed primarily to investigate these questions of administration and finance, and it did make a very careful and exhaustive examination into these matters. As a result of that examination the commission report condemned the system of annual parliamentary grants on which the corporation would have largely to rely.

Let anyone who receives this public trust know now that he will be required to account to the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament as the representatives of the Canadian people for his stewardship, that his operations and profits will be fully examined, and that there will be no hesitation in revoking a licence improperly granted or badly used.
I do not quarrel for one moment with the idea of the closest possible scrutiny of the affairs of the C.B.C. I am sure that must be done with respect to the C.B.C. If it is not done there will be extravagance, undoubtedly. Once the C.B.C. is given some kind of basic financial security perhaps that will necessitate an even stricter examination into its financial and administrative arrangements. Certainly the views of our party on this matter are well known, but I should like to put them briefly on the record once more.

(1)	We regard the C.B.C. as an essential and vital element in our attempt to create a united Canadian nation with a distinct national identity and culture.
(2)	We recognize and accept the existence of private radio and television stations, but only as integral parts of a single national broadcasting system, subject to controls and standards of performance designed to provide maximum service to the Canadian people. These private stations must not become a happy hunting ground for a favoured few who have received rare public assets in order to create large private profits.
(3)	We have every desire and intention that the C.B.C. should be required to operate efficiently and without waste of public moneys, and within a budget that will be fixed for longer than a year. But, subject to this, we believe that we should be prepared to pay nationally for the national service we wish to have and the national values we are seeking to maintain and strengthen.
(4)	We believe that the C.B.C. should be an independent agency, subject only to broad policy controls by parliament, free from political intervention by anyone and free also from stultifying and picayune interference with the details of its day to day programming operations. We believe its management must be free enough and strong enough to reject political interference with its programming, especially with its talks and public opinion programs, for whatever quarter it might come.
(5)	We believe that such an independent agency, sufficiently but not extravagantly financed and efficiently but not extravagantly operated, can be a major contributor to the development of a distinctive Canadian culture and to our growing sense of national identity.
I know the minister will agree wholeheartedly with me in that stated purpose of the national broadcasting system. We believe that such a system can help tie together the many scattered elements of Canada into a national unity. It can interpret the skills and aspirations and even the dreams of one part of Canada to other, distant parts. I think the C.B.C. is making a magnificient contribution to that end at the present time.
We also believe that this kind of national system can encourage musicians and artists and thinkers and entertainers and athletes to develop their varied talents and remain here in Canada for our entertainment and enlightenment. It can do much to build a Canadian culture-using that much misunderstood word in its widest and most imaginative sense-and to resist undesirable United States cultural influences which flow
Supply-National Revenue across our air waves, pervade our movie houses, and are to be found in books and magazines.
I do not want to be misunderstood in this. In this United States cultural impact there is much which may be and indeed is of very great value and adds richness to our Canadian life and from which we can and do benefit. But we must also have in Canada thoughts and ideas and music and entertainment of our own. Without this-and we cannot have it without a public broadcasting agency maintained at considerable public cost-we cannot have a Canadian nation at all.
Because it has a direct bearing on this point and is very well put, perhaps I should conclude by reading a few lines from an editorial in Maclean's magazine of July 18. After mentioning the differences, difficulties, controversies and anxieties created in recent months about broadcasting, the editorial states:
All this points to one of two conclusions:
On the one hand the C.B.C. management may be giving way to pressures that stronger men would ignore-which would be a grave fault in C.B.C. management.
On the other hand political pressures and even pressures from its own employees may be vastly greater than they used to be. too great for men of ordinary strength to resist-which would be a grave reproach to the politicians now in office.
It is extremely important for Canadians to know which, if either, of these conclusions is correct. For no matter who runs the national broadcasting system, Canada still needs one as much as ever- a system that will be not only genuinely Canadian but also genuinely free.
I state that if it is not genuinely free it will not be genuinely Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, the idea of a nation is a fragile one. It seems to me it has its origin not in forms, legal or otherwise, but in the consciousness of the people. Forms are the clothing of the nation, but the essence of nationality is psychological. It consists in a miraculous psychological transference from the circumscribed conception of family and locality, of deep affection for kitchen and home-the village pump, if you will-to the individual's identification of himself with the whole community.
This immense psychological link would be impossible if the conception of our national entity remained an abstract one. I know it is nurtured by symbols, but also by the continuing assurance of our separateness, our uniqueness. This is the vital and binding function of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to translate the abstract conception of nationhood into something that can be seen, heard, felt and understood. No organization has done more to achieve this high purpose.

An idea like distinctive nationality is not worth 5 cents on the dollar in the market place. You place the C.B.C. at the mercy of hucksters, of deodorant and detergent peddlers, and you wave goodbye to it as a buttress to national identity. If Sir John A. had been prepared to sacrifice the principle of national integrity to the claims of private enterprise there never would have been a C.P.R., nor would there have been that complex of Canadian private business which has managed to shelter itself within the national economic framework that Macdonald built. The vision of the entrepreneur, and of the petty and interested men who are prepared to help him, is limited to the area enclosed by the four corners of the dollar.
It is galling to me, and especially to someone interested in history, that the inheritors of the great Tory tradition of Macdonald have failed so dismally to learn the lesson he taught; that nationality for Canadians is something that must be paid for.
The committee's evidence dealing with the C.B.C. this year, Mr. Chairman, is over 700 pages in length. There were over 30 sittings. There was an agenda with dozens and dozens of points. How much time did the committee have to prepare the report? Over the week end. The draft report was prepared on Monday. A whole melange of ideas was chopped and meshed together, given a certain amount of coherence, a certain amount of balance, and then was put to the full committee in camera the next day. The committee spent somewhere between 21 hours and 31 hours sifting that particular melange of ideas into a rather stupid report which was presented to this house.
There were three great diversions at the sittings of this committee. I would like to just touch on them in the order of their appearance. The first diversion to me was the rather vicious destructiveness of those "men of the people" and of Maurice Duplessis who came into the committee and at almost every sitting identified themselves with the people and proceeded to present a form of questioning which indicated that they would like to have some kind of program control, or some kind of control over the appointments, almost a censorship, on one side of our national television and radio.
The second diversion of the committee meetings was the two sessions with the board of broadcast governors and with its head, Dr. Stewart. I say "diversion" because they took us to quite an extent out of the C.B.C. line, and I want to comment later on what we did find out, though it was not complete, about the board of broadcast governors.

The third diversion of the committee was the storm over the charge of clandestine political influence.
In so far as the first diversion is concerned, "les petits Canadiens", the chairman and the committee as a whole I think were rather leery, but they did make a final concession to them, one which certainly disgusted me, and that was the rather measly decision to delete any affirmation of the principles of the C.B.C. that might tie in historically with the fact that we had a Fowler commission and a Massey commission and other reports which were intimately connected with the committees of this house which were denied because, Mr. Chairman, "les petits Canadiens" did not care for them.
In so far as the board of broadcast governors is concerned, the evidence is not complete but there certainly was to me the suggestion that the board of broadcast governors is taking a fairly narrow, cautious way in working up and working out its functions and positions. There seems to be no real rapport yet with either the C.B.C. or with the private stations. So far the board of broadcast governors seems to be a body somewhat detached from the reality of a national, vital means of communication, and certainly so far there seems to be some confusion as to its functions.
So far as the charge of political interference is concerned, your committee investigated the charge that clandestine political influence was responsible for the cancellation of the program "Preview Commentary" and found no evidence to support the charge. Why? Why did they find no evidence? Because Mr. Bushnell denied the purport of what a number of people close to him said he said. Why? Because the Minister of National Revenue felt that he had no accurate recollection of any remarks he may have made about this program, "Preview Commentary".
In the unseemly rush past Mr. Bushnell's most peculiar and paradoxical evidence, we still have no explanation of the odd Celebrity Club phone call; the odd decision of the board of directors to support the management decision to use the axe, then the reversal of that decision. We also have the refusal of the committee majority to go further into these odd aspects.
What did the minister tell us? What stands out is that he dislikes this part of his job. Some commentary that is of the legislative aborting of last session that we produced on broadcasting. He wants out of the responsibility. This is what he said:
I told him-

That is Mr. Bushnell.
-I was going to try to get the Prime Minister to appoint someone else because 1 was sick and tired of these criticisms coming in from all over the country, from members of parliament, from my colleagues and from the public generally.
And from the C.C.F.

I continue:
I said that life was too short to be bothered with this thing and that I was going to get out of it.
Later, at page 604, we find the following:

I may have mentioned, and I undoubtedly have, many programs, sometimes commending him and sometimes criticizing him. I may have given my own personal opinion, and may have said: my colleagues are sore about this or irritated about that, or did appreciate that, or something of that kind. I have no power with the C.B.C. I am in the unfortunate position of receiving a lot of blame and having no responsibility for anything.
So those broad shoulders over there are just not broad enough, Mr. Chairman. What a commentary on the legislation; what an indication that we need the relationship of the C.B.C. to the government put in the way recommended by the Fowler commission; that is, from the C.B.C. to the B.B.G. and then the relationship to the government. Did the committee consider this evidence important, this evidence of the minister? Not at all. Let us tinker with the idea of a chairman distinct from the president. Perhaps that is a good suggestion but it is an evasion of the underlined fact that one of the grievous faults with the C.B.C. is its relationship with a minister who cannot take the C.B.C. in its relationship to him.
So far as political interference is concerned, the minister did give program criticism to Mr. Bushnell; he did mention that it came from his colleagues. Mr. Bushnell either did take this or some more mysterious information seriously enough that he jettisoned a fairly innocuous program without bothering to give those below him anything more than the compelling explanation "heads will roll". So this relatively innocuous program lasting three minutes and 11 seconds five days a week was axed, this nice little pin-money show for the boys in the gallery. We still do not know any more about the reasons for its going than that it was a mysterious aberration of Mr. Bushnell. We are afraid the committee's words that there was no evidence to support the charge has real substance. We are sure that the government members on the committee were none too anxious to search hard, Mr. Chairman. There may not now be anything rotten in Denmark, but there was something rotten in Denmark.
In so far as the C.B.C. budget is concerned, there are a number of ways in
Supply-National Revenue which the finances of the C.B.C. could be set up. One of the means we are using at the present time is a parliamentary appropriation. There is the possibility of a special tax-we have had that in the past-to support the C.B.C. There was the old possibility, used in the past, of licence fees supporting the C.B.C. We could have a parliamentary appropriation tied to a formula. It could be tied to the number of sets at so much a set; it could be a fixed percentage of the gross national product that would allow for changes and adjustments in the economy. It could be a fixed ratio to the population or to the population growth.
On this question of a formula or means of getting money for the C.B.C. we have an area where members of parliament do not need evidence so much as their own common sense and instinct as to what their electors and constituents would appreciate, what they themselves would think it is worth. Did we get anything constructive from this committee on that? No; we merely got the recommendation of some formula by which limits may be set on the annual contribution of the federal government to the corporation, plus this very peculiar addenda that increasing effort should be made to ensure the emergence of vigorous commercial policies.
What encouragement to a public corporation. Did socialists recommend this? No, sir; these were private enterprisers recommending that there should be increased effort to ensure the emergence of vigorous commercial policies on the part of a public corporation. This committee would not suggest a formula or possible formulae in an area where the situation was and is most grave, that having to do with the financial needs of the corporation.
But on sponsorship, that obsession of the hon. member for Calgary South, we got quite substantial recommendations. It is said to the C.B.C., "Be vigorous. Ease the taxpayer and belt that other face of the taxpayer, the consumer face, through more bites of the advertising dollar. Rob Paul to pay Paul". It is not the C.B.C.'s function to turn a profit. Where this can be done without impairing the C.B.C.'s prime function as a national service and without diminishing the standard of programming there can be no objection, but it is not the end goal of the C.B.C. to turn a profit. This is precisely the weakness in the proposition that the C.B.C. should cede production rights in sponsored shows. United States experience has shown that this leads to sponsor control of program content.
On that point I should like to recommend to all members, and especially the Conservative members, a speech by Edward R_

Supply-National Revenue Murrow delivered to the radio and television news directors' association last year. It is found in the November 13, 1958 issue of The Reporter. I am sure all hon. members realize that Mr. Murrow has been a prominent figure in United States television. He had this to say:
I am entirely persuaded that the American public is more reasonable, restrained, and more mature than most of our industry's program planners believe. Their fear of controversy is not warranted by the evidence. I have reason to know, as do many of you, that when the evidence on a controversial subject is fairly and calmly presented, the public recognizes it for what it is-an effort to illuminate rather than to agitate.
He goes on to say:
The oldest excuse of the networks for their timidity is their youth. Their spokesmen say: "We are young; we have not developed the traditions nor acquired the experience of the older media." If they but knew it, they are building those traditions, creating those precedents every day. Each time they yield to a voice from Washington or any political pressure, each time they eliminate something that might offend some section of the community, they are creating their own body of precedent and tradition. They are, in fact, not content to be "half safe."
Later on Mr. Murrow makes this statement:
It may be that the present system, with no modifications and no experiments, can survive. Perhaps the money-making machine has some kind of built-in perpetual motion, but I do not think so. . . . Our mass media reflect this. But unless we get up off our fat surpluses and recognize that television in the main is being used to distract, delude, amuse, and insulate us, then television and those who finance it, those who look at it and those who work at it, may see a totally different picture too late.
This is a commentary by a very intelligent man, Mr. Chairman, on the very thing that some members of the house and of the special committee seem to want to drive us toward. The United States system is not working out so well in this field that we can take the private entrepreneurs or private systems there as any great models for programming or sponsorship. It should be the business of the government to ensure that the C.B.C. needs as little sponsorship as possible. Can the C.B.C. be blamed when private corporations quite naturally take advantage of the weak financial position of the corporation? Is it likely that private corporations will be shamed into paying higher amounts merely as a result of the publication of program accounts? I think the answers to these questions are no.
The only way to rescue the C.B.C. is not through facile lip service to practicable formulae, which is sheer escapism, but by improving the bargaining position of the C.B.C. in a ruthless and predatory market by establishing it on the sound financial basis

that any great public service requires. I should like to ask those hon. members who are so antagonistic to the C.B.C. this question. Does the government subsidize the Department of External Affairs? In essence they are carrying out the same function.
The most disturbing element in what is going on in the country with respect to C.B.C. criticism is that there is a temptation for any one of us to climb on this band wagon. I say there is a temptation for any of us. There is a temptation to many of the people in my constituency who do not think of this greater entity and the need to preserve its uniqueness. In their desire to have wrestling three or four nights a week or to have canned westerns they are willing to go along. But I suggest that we have always to look at this national need for the C.B.C., and we have to consider the nature of the criticism of the C.B.C. that appears in public media.
I happen to follow the fortunes of the Thomson newspapers very closely. There are over 24 outlets in Canada that week after week pour out a daily dose of poison against the C.B.C. Mr. Thomson, whose progress in Britain I am sure will some day be rewarded by his becoming Lord Thomson of South Porcupine, started in the private broadcasting business and made a great success. There is nothing against that at all, but he has gone on to build an empire of newspapers, radio and television interests that surely makes him or his newspapers less than fair commentators on the position of the C.B.C.
One can say the same thing about the Sifton interests. Those of us who follow what the Siftons and Mr. Bell are doing could become very worried about the situation in Regina or the situation in Winnipeg, where we may be moving toward a private monopoly in newspapers, radio and television. I should like to remind hon. members and the people of the country, if they do happen to listen, that much of the criticism of the C.B.C. in the newspaper medium is of the orientation of the Thomson and Sifton interests, which are about as interested in Canadian nationalism as-well, I don't know what to say to convey their self-interest. Certainly they are much more interested in their connections with their newspapers and their television and radio stations.
On the question of the board of broadcast governors, the legislation produced last year has been most disappointing. To me the evidence given by Dr. Stewart before the committee was most disappointing. He had to be prodded into saying that the board of broadcast governors was anything more than a passive instrument that just waited. From the minister's statement last year we had

hopes that the board of broadcast governors would really enunciate a national policy, that it would be the body that would determine the carrying out of this marriage between the C.B.C. and the private stations in one national system, that it would determine how this was going to come about. But we have not much promise in the indications that we get.
Admittedly it was incomplete, but I suggest that in the interval from when this session ends until the next one opens the minister, if he has any influence or any interest left, should try to encourage the board of broadcast governors to give the leadership that it seems hesitant about giving now so far as a national policy is concerned.
Are we going to go on, Mr. Chairman?

I assume we are going through the lunch hour. The final point in a general way that I should like to make relates to the Prime Minister and the members of the government, I mean members of the government as a whole. I have to be fair to a number of Conservative members with whom I worked on the committee and say I think they have caught that kind of vision the Prime Minister has presented to this country, a vision of Canadianism. However, I am very much afraid that many members in that government group have not caught its meaning.
We have a Prime Minister who makes a point of Canadianism, who makes a point about the commonwealth and its importance. In essence, in two elections he fought campaigns that were based, at least partly, on the statement that we will take a firm stand with the United States. It is no good, in so far as the C.B.C. is concerned, taking a firm stand with the United States in an official way because the need is still there, more than ever before, to see how the C.B.C. fits in with the private stations to stem that influence from the south. The need is perhaps greater than it has been in the past; the need is not less.
The Leader of the Opposition made the point that the Liberal party still stood for the C.B.C. fitting into a system with the private stations, essentially as a national policy. He made the point that the C.B.C. must be efficient, even though it cannot pay its way. He made the point that the board of broadcast governors and the C.B.C. should work within a particular national policy. Well, on every one of those points I think we agree. I do not know how many members of the government agree with this. The Leader
Supply-National Revenue of the Opposition made a point about these lucrative plums that are going to be handed out, and how we are all going to be watching whether some of the so-called pals of the government get these plums.
He also made a point in connection with the C.B.C.'s position which he said may be in jeopardy because of the impact of this competition. Well, I believe that is the kind of chore the board of broadcast governors should be carrying out now, examining this sort of problem and planning to give leadership. I can see that in the rich television markets alone which we have concentrated in about four places in Canada we are not going to get the national service that any contribution from those market areas in terms of advertising revenues would warrant.
One of the ironies we always forget in talking about the competitive nature of private stations, that they will get in there and fight, is that there was never a case of which I know in the history of all the applications made to the C.B.C. in the past when it was the regulatory agency where, if there was one private station in an area and some other group wanted to put in another private station, there was a welcome mat put out. This is how free and enterprising these private enterprises are. They never put the welcome mat out. They fought over the application that was made. These are the ones who have been talking about the C.B.C. monopoly and its dangers, but when it comes down to the point of really believing in the principle they merely yap about it. Now they want protection for their monopoly, right down the line.
Some hon. members will say that is the nature of the market. Sure it is, but then don't yap. We have had this history of yapping against the C.B.C. on this point, and this will be a key point in the future. We have a private television station in Port Arthur, and there are a number of them across the country linked with the C.B.C. network, doing a fair to middling job, sometimes a good job. I want to say that if we are going to turn the C.B.C. open to competition, I hope the C.B.C. will take a good, long look at the prospect of firing a few more of their projected television stations into these little empires. Then will we ever hear the yapping.
The whole situation with respect to the C.B.C. may well be determined in the next six or eight months by the kind of mood and attitude that develops daily and is given enunciation by this government. I have so much respect for the minister, both in personal terms and the kind of character he has, that I am still hoping, despite his desire

Those who may think they are little Canadians, who think you are going to solve everything by turning it over to the private broadcasters, should look at the evidence given before the royal commissions, should look at the evidence given before house committees, and they will see what kind of service the private broadcasters will give us. There is no doubt, and I think any fair-minded Canadian would admit it, of the need for the C.B.C. If it has had a time of trouble, some of the responsibility rests upon the legislation which was introduced last year by this government.
We would welcome nothing more than a statement, not from the minister but from the Prime Minister himself, on what he believes and thinks about the C.B.C. and its position in the future. I think that would do more to handle what concerns me most within the framework of this house, that is the niggling, nasty desire amongst some Conservative members to junk the C.B.C. I believe there is a great need for the Prime Minister to lay it on the line so that all the members of his party will realize that junking the C.B.C. is not Conservative policy.

Mr. Chairman, while we were discussing the business of the C.B.C.,
I wanted, to express some of my views in order to rectify a few wrong impressions and throw some light upon the principles which, to my mind, should guide that corporation.
I am sorry that the impending conclusion of this session will stop us from dealing at length with the extremely important question of the C.B.C.
I would, as I said before, rectify some wrong impressions resulting from speeches we have heard. As far as I am concerned, I maintain that I never had, and that I have not today any intention of destroying the C.B.C. or of minimizing in any way the prestige acquired by that corporation. I had the opportunity, on some other occasion in this house, to praise the C.B.C. and to mention its excellent achievements. I thought, Mr. Chairman, that this would not deprive me of the right to criticize and to suggest possible improvements in some of the less creditable work of the C.B.C.


During the investigation by the parliamentary committee on radio and television, which I attended as frequently as possible, I tried in every way to obtain information which would help me evaluate properly the former achievements of the C.B.C. and its policy with regard to the future. I had an opportunity during that investigation to express my lack of satisfaction and, in some ways, my discontent, with regard to answers that had been given to me by those responsible for the C.B.C. If I expressed that discontent and that lack of satisfaction, Mr. Chairman, I did not do so in order to minimize the significance of the corporation and to weaken its prestige, but because I thought that my sense of responsibility and the sense of responsibility of the representatives of the people imposed the duty upon us-and a very serious duty at that-of enquiring about everything which goes on in the C.B.C. We should do so, first of all in order to dispel certain misunderstandings, and also to answer the numerous representations received from the taxpayers in the past, and which are still coming in today.
Before the session comes to an end, I did not want to leave hon. members of this house or members of the press gallery under the wrong impression, which the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) tried to create, as did, up to a certain point, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson).
I had prepared some notes of a very moderate character. I tried to apply to my remarks in this house a proper sense of measure. But I feel that, in view of the attacks directed against us, we could not very well limit ourselves to general remarks, but should rather refute, to a certain extent, the false statements made a few moments ago.
Mr. Chairman, at no time during the investigation did the committee, or representatives of the province of Quebec, try to advance a political cause. They simply tried to reply to the public's request that full light be thrown on the C.B.C. operations, not because the people, as a whole, thought there were scandals in the C.B.C., but because they thought that the situation in that state organization was sufficiently serious to warrant an investigation.
It is in that spirit that we undertook to work in the parliamentary committee on radio and television. We never tried, in any way- and I challenge anyone to say the contrary-

we never tried, as I say, to advance political views. We strictly adhered to facts, and public facts. And in that connection, I believe it is proper to recall here an incident which occurred during the investigation.
The committee had decided, from the start, not to make any personalities. For my part,
I was never opposed to such a procedure in the committee; I do think, however, that such a procedure could not prevent us from referring to responsible persons and mentioning public facts involving the C.B.C. administration in any one of its sectors.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the attitude of Quebec members, during the investigation of the parliamentary committee on radio and television, was one of responsible representatives of the people who, considering the amounts of money engulfed into the C.B.C., are strictly and conscientiously entitled to wonder what the C.B.C. is doing with that money, and I repeat, not with a view to uncovering scandals nor to insinuate that there were misappropriations, but simply in view of establishing that the money entrusted to the people responsible for the C.B.C. is well administered and yields the returns which can be normally expected.
Mr. Chairman, I must say, as I have repeated time and again during the proceedings of the parliamentary committee on radio and television, that I was not satisfied with the replies we were given, because I found them evasive, and I found also that the points we raised were not answered properly.
Mr. Chairman, before going into my remarks to the house, I wanted to make that point, so that there will be no mistake about the attitude of Quebec members who sat on the committee on broadcasting.
I also expressed the view that we should divide the parliamentary committee on broadcasting into two sections, so as to give separate consideration to the problems of both networks, the French and the English, which really have different problems and should be dealt with differently. Such a division was rejected for reasons of procedure, but I think it is too bad, because in view of the tremendous task facing us, we were unable to do a thorough enough job of getting at the information we needed.
Mr. Chairman, I was saying a moment ago that we tried to live up to our true responsibilities. I base this statement on the principles
Supply-National Revenue of responsible government. Every year, we are asked to vote money to the C.B.C. This money is provided not by the members of the house, not by members of the C.B.C., but by the people generally. It is supplied by the hon. members, by officials of the C.B.C. and by each and every taxpayer. So we have a legitimate right, Mr. Chairman, to inquire whether this money is being properly used.
We tried to find out how the C.B.C. is managed financially. Other hon. members who are better qualified than I am to deal with the technical aspect of such problems, will discuss that point. The report submitted by the parliamentary committee on broadcasting contains a number of recommendations on this score.
I shall not go into that, however, because it would take too much time, and besides, it is beyond the scope of my humble qualifications. However, Mr. Chairman, I would point out, as I pointed out during the proceedings, that the C.B.C. should not be regarded as just another crown corporation.
The C.B.C. has nothing in common with an administration such as the C.N.R., because the C.B.C. does not deal merely in material things, but must take into account a moral and intellectual content. People with different outlooks take a different stand on this matter. If you restrict the committee's responsibility merely to the financial aspect of the C.B.C., where problems are translated into figures and accounting formulas, the parliamentary committee's discussion should have been restricted to administrative problems, inasmuch as they have budgetary implications.
But if, on the contrary, it is realized that the C.B.C. is not a crown corporation like others, and that it does not deal only with material matters, but that it involves, as I said earlier, a vast and important moral and intellectual content, it cannot be dealt with like a strictly financial organization. Thus, the parliamentary committee which deals with the C.B.C. is entitled-and this without interfering in internal affairs of the corporation- to try to establish a relationship between the cost of the C.B.C. to the taxpayers and what the corporation offers them.
It is in that light that I have tried to contain my remarks, and it is for that reason that, during the inquiry, I have tried to get information on the general policy of the C.B.C., especially in the matter of programming.

Today, Mr. Chairman, right or wrong the C.B.C.'s business is not only informatory but cultural and even goes as far as being educational.
I therefore have the right, as a representative of the people, to ask who are those responsible for educational activities at the C.B.C. today. When, right or wrong, it seeks as I say, to educate the people, I am entitled to wonder what their principles are, their moral standards, and their line of thought in general. I have a right to ask whether those people may, by all sorts of means, reasonably appeal to the judgment of the people with regard to politics, by setting up at the taxpayer's expense political hustings persistently aiming at the destruction of governments. I have a right to know- and I am speaking for myself as a taxpayer -whether those people would necessarily be accepted in our educational institutions. I have a right to ask whether they are qualified to look after popular education, and even education period.
That is the spirit in which I asked my questions at the meetings of the committee on broadcasting. But I wanted to know exactly what future part the C.B.C. would play in the field of public education.
I tried to obtain some information in order clearly to establish what were the intellectual and moral standards of those responsible for the educational aspect of the C.B.C. I was told that the corporation tried to present programs that were morally sound. Isn't that just wonderful, Mr. Chairman? Can it do other than strive to present morally sound programs?
I am saying that, Mr. Chairman, without in any way trying to minimize the significance of the beautiful and valuable programs put on by the C.B.C. What I am saying is that there is, at the C.B.C., an atmosphere-I am more particularly speaking now of the French network-an atmosphere of amorality. During the survey, something was said about immoral shows. For my part, I believe that the C.B.C. has enough decency not to present any shows that are immoral. But I think that there is at the C.B.C., please note that I am indicting nobody whatsoever, but I wonder whether people responsible for those programs are acting deliberately-a certain lack of moral sense, precisely because there is no moral reference which might be a guide with regard to some of the programs.


I also maintain, Mr. Chairman, that all those who want to call Quebec educational institutions into account are not enough concerned about the national character of C.B.C. programs. There, we have a national institution which has first of all to convey national culture, besides supervising with the greatest care everything coming from outside this country.
The aim would not be to prohibit an access to universal culture to our people, Mr. Chairman, but it must be considered that the public at whom the C.B.C. programs are aimed is not always a discerning one, and is often unable to distinguish what really pertains to Canadian tradition, and what belongs to other cultural expressions.
Mr. Chairman, those issues of a moral and educational character are of capital importance, and hon. members of this house, and particularly members of the parliamentary committee on broadcasting, have no right to feel unconcerned in that respect.
During the convention on radio and television broadcasting, which took place a few day ago in Montreal, His Eminence Cardinal Leger stated the following:
The convention, he said, does not propose to condemn anything. Rather, it tends to express the views of the people. Radio and television are exerting some influence in every home and the church is therefore interested in those means of expression which, today, have become almost indispensable. Everyone has certainly the right to say what he thinks with regard to those programs.
Mr. Chairman, it is not exerting any political pressure to express one's opinions on C.B.C. programs	And I do not think
there has ever been a better court in this respect than the committee on broadcasting for finding out about the spirit of a corporation, the responsible executives of which are often not close enough to the people for whom the programs are meant. It would be difficult to know the views of the man in the street, if those who represent the corporation are not in close enough contact with him. Yet, they should take their inspiration from the people for programs pertaining to Canadian culture with French and Christian cultural backgrounds.
There has been talk of political interference, there have ben persistent suggestions of political interference, in an attempt to give the impression that only Conservative members from the province of Quebec were trying to interfere politically.

Mr. Chairman, there are citizens who complain about C.B.C. news commentaries because they feel those commentaries are controlled and that news commentary programs are monopolized by people representing a particular form and school of thought.
I have no objection, Mr. Chairman, to each citizen expressing his views. I have no objection to organized groups being given a chance to express themselves. What I do oppose is that to news commentaries be always entrusted to the same representatives, the same groups of thought.
To any who would charge political interference in C.B.C. news services, I can read a document proving that political interference does not necessarily come from the quarters they think. I have here a C.B.C. document bearing the signature of Mr. Marcel Ouimet. It is addressed to the news editors in Toronto, to the regional director and to several other directors of the French network. The document, dated July 6, 1959 comes from Ottawa, and reads as follows:
What strikes me Is that, as a result of certain circumstances, we seem to be giving special emphasis to statements by ministers of the provincial government. For instance, I do not believe we were justified, last May 24, to give ten minutes of "Camera 59" to extracts from the speech of premier Duplessis at the convention of electricians in Three Rivers.
Those who were attacked by the provincial leader that day did not have, so far as I know, an equal opportunity to defend themselves.
The same could be said of the speech made by Mr. Sauve a few weeks ago in Montreal.
Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to efforts being made to reach what they call, in the C.B.C., a balance of opinions, but I do not believe that a C.B.C. news official should not have the right to object to opinions being expressed during the news by a man who, after all, is the premier of the provincial state.
I should like to refer also, Mr. Chairman, to a document which will be appended in the latest record of the committee on broadcasting, a letter from a parliamentary correspondent of he Droit, Mr. Chaloult, stating that he had to refuse C.B.C. programs, that he had to refuse to make comments over the air because he had been asked to make comments favourable to the party then in power. If that is not political interference, Mr. Chairman, we might as well do away with the word, and the concept which
Supply-National Revenue remains in the minds of people who have charged the government with being guilty of interference.
Mr. Chairman, I come back to the claim made a moment ago that the actions of Conservative members have jeopardized the C.B.C. I do not believe that public opinion, which expresses itself mainly through its legitimate representatives, could jeopardize a body such as the C.B.C. As I said just now, and I have full confidence in the C.B.C. I do believe that the C.B.C. is able to give us excellent services. But I feel that the danger which now threatens the C.B.C. does not lie in attacks by members of the house or by various citizens, but in the lack of ability which, in my opinion, prevails in several administrative departments of the C.B.C. And please mark my words: I am not condemning the C.B.C. as a whole, because there are, on C.B.C. staff, excellent people, people of genuine ability in their field, but I also believe that, in some particularly strategic departments, some people are incompetent. I do not hesitate to use the word incompetent. It is that incompetence which threatents the C.B.C.
At the conclusion of its proceedings, the parliamentary committee submitted a report. That report, Mr. Chairman, includes excellent recommendations. For my part, I believe that all those recommendations are valid, but I also believe that the report, inasmuch as it recommends structural and organizational reforms within the C.B.C., is perhaps premature. I believe that the investigation we just made, and that the crisis the C.B.C. has gone through these last few months, require that we give increased attention to C.B.C. administration. I believe that it calls, on the part of the people's representatives and on the part of all those who are directly concerned with the C.B.C., for much reflection, and for study of all we have learned in the committee on broadcasting; yes a detailed study of the C.B.C.'s general policy as expressed in the documents submitted to us by the C.B.C. itself during the investigation and which could certainly allow us to introduce recommendations covering the whole activity of the C.B.C., its purposes, objectives, and responsibilities to the public.
For my part, I believe it is imperative to revise very carefully, the C.B.C. plans and objectives, in order to determine exactly what the C.B.C.'s responsibility should be in matters of education. I don't say that it must have that responsibility, but it could have it.

Supply-National Revenue
Before proceeding to an overall shake-up of the C.B.C., to drastic structural reforms, I believe we should study all those documents we now have on hand, and that we should also study the recommendations which were made by those citizens gathered in convention in Montreal a few days ago. There is talk of a controlling body, a body which, let's call it by its name, would be a censorship body, and which would be responsible for the supervision of the moral and intellectual aspects of C.B.C. programs.
I repeat, for my part, the suggestion I made last year about the competence of those who are responsible for news and cultural programs in the C.B.C. I suggested then that consideration should be given to organizing competitions, as well as to organizing professional schools which would allow all those interested in radio and T.V. business to acquire a reasonable degree of competence, based on adequate culture.
Finally, before I close my remarks, Mr. Chairman, allow me to emphasize once more that the C.B.C. should give young writers all possible help, and remove all dangers of monopoly, in avoiding the maintenance, for years on end, of the same programs, which is obviously a handicap to young writers and a danger also to writers who, for years, have been favoured by the C.B.C.
I also insist that the C.B.C. give Canadian artists all possible opportunities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have been listening closely and with interest to the speech just made by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay). He started off by saying he would correct some false impressions that may have been left by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who spoke before him.
He said, among other things, that the allegations of these two members were untrue. However, I was here during the speeches of those two hon. members and in my view, they said nothing untrue.
Moreover, if they had said anything untrue, the -hon. member for Roberval had a right, under standing orders, to rise and raise an objection, and to call for a withdrawal of the statements made by the hon. members.
I did not have to rise.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am saying that the hon. member was fully entitled,
[Mr. Tremblay.)
under standing orders, to rise on a point of privilege when he felt he was being personally referred to. However, in his remarks, the hon. member has altogether failed to prove that an hon. member had in any way made untrue allegations about him.
Yet, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) indicated, with his slight English accent, that some members who took part in the proceedings of the broadcasting committee were petty Canadians.
Slight accent! He didn't know what he was talking about.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the allegations of the hon. member for Port Arthur apply to the hon. member for Roberval, let him accept them. In my view, the speech we have just heard bears the imprint of a petty Canadian. It seems to me that this is not the type of speech that should be made in this house by a broad-minded educator.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to devote more time to the statements of the hon. member for Roberval, because I have other remarks to make with regard to the matter before the house. However, I shall come back to that later.
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to repeat what was said by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) concerning the general attitude of the Liberal party with regard to broadcasting in Canada. That policy was established not only by the Leader of the Opposition in this house, but it was set out many times by our party when we sat on the other side of the house. There has been no change in that policy, because we have always favoured protecting this government agency.
However, I wish to recall briefly some statements that were repeated many times by all major groups in the province of Quebec, and particularly at sittings of the Massey and Fowler commissions. Such groups have repeatedly asserted that the C.B.C. was and should remain an essential instrument for the progress and expansion of French Canadian culture, not only within the province of Quebec, but in all parts of Canada where there are important French-speaking groups.
This essential contribution has worked at two separate levels. First, it has enabled our artists and writers to devote themselves

more completely to their art, so much so that one might say the fresh impetus noted in the arts, in literature and music, for several years now, in the province of Quebec was indirectly but most surely brought about, to a large extent, by the C.B.C.
Moreover, the C.B.C., through its programs, many of which are broadcast not only in Quebec but throughout Canada, has enabled many people who otherwise would have been unable to do so, to share in this renewal of culture, and to enjoy themselves while so doing.
Mr. Chairman, in recalling the special contribution of the C.B.C., I know I am expressing the majority opinion of those who, in the province of Quebec, are interested in things of the mind. Who would have thought, two years ago, that today we would be faced with attacks of a scope of which we are perfectly aware, against the C.B.C.
In making these remarks, I would not like to give the impression, however, that everything is perfect in the C.B.C., as far as administration and programming are concerned. In such a complex and difficult field, one must admit it is impossible to please everyone at the same time. It is even possible, as it happened recently, that serious mistakes may be made. It is possible that some programs which gave rise to serious attacks on the part of the great majority of the population of Quebec-I am sure-do appear on television, and it is also normal that the competent authorities should vehemently denounce such errors, as they did recently, in order to avoid their recurrence.
What I do not accept, however, is that such errors should give rise to scandals and protests from people who are now trying to sow public immorality in the province of Quebec by every means at their disposal.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The fact remains that despite some mistakes, the C.B.C. has done a magnificent job-
Specify.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-which should be continued and extended. The C.B.C. is one of our main bulwarks against cultural invasion from the United States. Indeed I did indicate in a number of instances, when sitting on the other side of the house-the Leader of the Opposition mentioned this again this
Supply-National Revenue morning-that the C.B.C. is our strongest defence against the invasion of our culture by United States programs. Despite the important contributions of our institutions of learning and other instruments of culture, Canada's cultural future would be gravely jeopardized without the existence and continued progress of the C.B.C.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that every member in this house, at least those sitting on this side, will bear this testimony to the C.B.C.
Now sir-

What testimony?
(Text):

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Now, sir, to continue to fulfill its vital role and to progress as we think it should, the C.B.C. needs two things. It needs, first of all, money, and it needs independence. Some members of the committee are surprised, and in fact they are even scandalized, at the annual deficits of the C.B.C. I have no doubt-and I am sure the committee is of the same view-that substantial savings could be made by more efficient administration. I want to emphasize, however, that in a country like Canada the C.B.C. would not fulfil its role if it were not incurring substantial deficits. I would go even further and say that I would be against the C.B.C. if it were to become solely a profitable organization, because that would mean that it would not accomplish the purpose for which it was established.
The deficit this year, as the committee knows, is some $51 million. This is, of course, a tremendous amount of money. However, when we look at what we are spending each year to defend our culture and our institutions against possible aggression we should come to the conclusion, it seems to me, sir, that the amounts we devote to our cultural enjoyment and development are very small indeed.
The major threat faced by the C.B.C. at the present time, however, concerns its independence, its freedom from political interference. We are not always conscious of the fact that there are two different aspects to this question and this threat. In the first place there is the manifestation of political interference itself. In the second place, there is the way in which those who are chiefly responsible for C.B.C. management react to that threat.
Political interference is certainly a most undesirable thing. I do not believe there is

Supply-National Revenue anyone in this committee who will gainsay that statement, but it is disastrous when C.B.C. management and those associated with it comply with such interference. There is no more effective method of destroying the C.B.C. than by transforming it into a political instrument of the government, and that is what those of us who sit here, as well as those who sit in the small group at the other end, want to make sure will not occur. That is why the most important responsibility of the C.B.C. is to resist that kind of interference.
I admit that it is not an easy matter. I admit that under the circumstances in which we find ourselves sometimes it is extremely difficult to resist pressure. Parliament, however, and the Canadian people have repeatedly decided that the C.B.C. would not accomplish a useful purpose if it were not free from governmental political interference, clandestine or otherwise.
That freedom, sir, and that independence which are so essential to the cultural welfare of the Canadian people have been entrusted by parliament to the C.B.C., and it is the major responsibility of its officials to preserve and maintain those essential requirements of that public service. The independence of the C.B.C. is as important to our democracy as academic freedom in our universities and other teaching institutions. It is as important for the officials of the C.B.C. to maintain the independence of that institution and to fight for it, if necessary, as it is for university authorities and university professors to preserve academic freedom.
To preserve those great democratic values may require at times, from those who are entrusted with the safeguarding of those values, a tremendous amount of courage and even the sacrifice of their jobs and their careers. However, our democracy expects those sacrifices from them because they have accepted those important responsibilities, and they must now live up to them. That is why all the C.B.C. officials who recently decided to resign over the issue of "Preview Commentary" have won our admiration for the courage they showed on that occasion. As far as we are concerned, here in this house, it is our duty to protect and support those people in the C.B.C. who carry these responsibilities and who resist political interference, even risking their careers to do that which they rightfully feel and believe is their duty.
The safeguarding of the independence of the C.B.C. has not been entrusted only to its

management. It is also the duty of the government to respect that freedom, and we have good reason to believe that the government has failed in that duty.
There are still widespread rumours that there was direct interference in connection with the radio program "Preview Commentary". Apparently the real story of this dramatic incident has not yet been told. It is widely reported that the Prime Minister himself advised-I use that word because it was used before-the Minister of National Revenue that his head and that of Mr. Bush-nell would roll if that program was not dropped immediately-
That is tommyrot.
Irresponsible gossip.
Where is the evidence?
We were not allowed to get the evidence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -advice which it is reported was communicated to Mr. Bushnell, who informed several C.B.C. officials of it. Well, Mr. Chairman, there has been a great protest from the other side of the house in connection with that statement, and there has been an endeavour in the report of the committee to whitewash that affirmation completely, notwithstanding the evidence which was given in that respect.
Where is the evidence?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The least that should be done by those who are in office and those who are responsible for this series of events is to deny that suggestion and put the position of the government clearly before the house.
I want to leave that matter now and deal with the French network of the C.B.C. According to similar reports the independence of the French network of the C.B.C. would appear to be in greater danger than the English network. We all remember, of course, the most unfortunate incidents which occurred in Montreal at the beginning of the year. On that occasion the Minister of National Revenue was quite unfair, I submit with deference, to the employees and especially to the producers of the French network in Montreal. At that time he blamed the producers for the dispute. His statement will be found on pages 775 and 776 of Hansard for February 6, when he said:
I also want to pay tribute, Mr. Chairman, to the management of the C.B.C. for the way in which they have conducted themselves during this strike. This has been the most unfortunate and unnecessary episode in labour relations in Canadian history, in my opinion. It is something which never should have happened.

He also made other accusations against the producers. However, about six months later, during the course of the committee meeting on July 2, when the minister appeared before the special committee on broadcasting he had changed his mind. As found at page 605 of the proceedings, in referring to the top management of the C.B.C. he had this to say:
Going back over these other occasions, like the Algerian matter, the Mother d'Youville question, the case of the person being brought in from Europe and also the background of the strike, where I was told afterwards if they had exercised any control here, the strike would not have happened, I probably told them, "You had better tighten up this organization or something will happen to somebody around here."
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister says "Hear, hear", so there is no denying this statement. The minister therefore admitted before the committee that he learned afterwards that if management in Ottawa had exercised any control the dispute would not have developed. The minister was quite wrong earlier and it seems to me that in so far as the producers involved in the Montreal dispute are concerned he owes them an apology and should make amends to them.
In connection with this whole matter concerning the French television network I want to refer to an article by Mr. Mark Harrison of the Toronto Star.
(Translation):
Why don't you read the pastoral letter from our bishops?

speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me the time, I intend to put on the record-

Address yourself to the
Chairman of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
-what religious authorities have said at a conference which was held not long ago.
