Evidently, Mr. Chairman, what I am saying is not appreciated by the hon. members who are continually interrupting. They do not like the fact that we have been saying repeatedly that in the province of Quebec they have been interfering with the management of the C.B.C. Why? Because some of the commentators have been disagreeing with statements made by themselves and by other government members. I should like to come back to the article by Mr. Mark Harrison published in the Toronto Star of July 2. It reads in part as follows:
Nowhere is the C.B.C. more exposed to political pressure than in the French network in Quebec. Surrounded by hostile politicians, C.B.C. producers 66968-9-400
Supply-National Revenue in Montreal have been continually harassed in the past two years by attempts to undermine the independence of the corporation. The pressures have come from old C.B.C. adversaries-Duplessis supporters emboldened by the entrenchment of a Conservative administration in Ottawa. They have also come from the new Quebec Conservative M.P.'s who appear to assume their parliamentary status entitles them to influence policy in the corporation.
How do they apply these pressures against the C.B.C.? Mostly in a covert manner, seeking to make their influence felt through the federal cabinet, primarily through Solicitor General Leon Balcer and Senate Speaker Mark Drouin.
Last winter, for example, two confidential documents, blasting the talks and public affairs branch of the C.B.C.'s French network, were prepared by a group of Quebec Conservatives and submitted to the government. The documents have never been made public but it is understood they contained two major indictments:
1.	That the C.B.C. Montreal group was riddled with left wingers.
2.	That a few favoured commentators were appearing too frequently on the C.B.C. in Montreal.
The commentators to whom the Conservative M.P.'s objected were men like Jean Louis Gagnon, editor of La Presse, Gerard Pelletier of the Catholic syndicates and Andre Laurendeau, an editor of he Devoir. The documents were passed on to the C.B.C. and the French network officials were required to submit reports which, in fact, were rebuttals of the charges.
I have not the time to read the questions and answers made by the minister responsible for the C.B.C. concerning this matter, but he did not deny the statement contained in that editorial. We have, therefore, good reason to believe that some of these pressures and some of these representations have been successful. Thus it has been decided to drop the program "Point de Mire", which had been tremendously popular and a tremendous success, by Rene Levesque. What justified that decision? Was it the fact that Mr. Levesque participated actively in the Montreal strike for which the producers and artists were not mainly responsible, according to the minister's new version? Surely this would not be acceptable. Was the program abandoned because some Quebec Conservative members, like the hon. member for Roberval, did not like Mr. Levesque? This would be most unfair.
Personally I do not know what the party affiliations of Mr. Levesque are, and this has nothing to do with the present situation. I do know, however, that Mr. Levesque is an objective commentator. I do know that he is a man who knows international and national subjects, and that he is listened to very carefully by a large part of the population of the province of Quebec. The proof of that lies in the fact that in the survey which was made of French television programs, it was "Point de Mire" which topped the list.

Who made the survey?

Supply-National Revenue

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Why then, I ask, was it decided to discontinue this program? We are certainly entitled to a full explanation of this from those who are responsible. Was it because some Conservative members from the province of Quebec complained that he was being seen too often on television? This is a complaint we hear very often, as was stated to us by the hon. member for Roberval.
What is the matter with an individual appearing often on television, provided he is able to entertain and give the public what they want? After all, you cannot take a man off the C.B.C. television network because of the fact that he has a wide and varied experience, and supplant him by another who has little or no experience, until that other has attained such experience. The complaint in itself is no justification whatever. The only acceptable criterion in this respect is whether the commentator is sufficiently interesting to keep his audience, and whether the program is achieving a useful purpose. It would be most regrettable if the C.B.C. had to drop its most popular French programs simply because of asinine arguments made by members such as the hon. member for Roberval.
In the last analysis the public should be the final judge of this question, because the function of the C.B.C. is to serve the public, not to satisfy the vengeance of political parties and members of parliament. I admit the C.B.C. should try, and it certainly did in the past, to develop new talent. However, it would be ridiculous if the C.B.C. had to drop artists and commentators as soon as they have acquired experience. The C.B.C., I am told, has not asked Mr. Levesque to continue his program "Point de Mire". This is unfair not only to him but also to the public who liked his presentation in the province of Quebec. This decision cannot be explained otherwise than by political interference, and I ask the minister to tell the house what has happened in this connection. Such pressures have also resulted in the dropping of other programs and other regular commentators from the French network of the C.B.C.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If it is utter nonsense, as the minister has interjected, why has the program not been reinstated in the same manner as "Preview Commentary" has been? There has, no doubt, been some kind of interference in connection with "Point de Mire" and other programs on the C.B.C., as there was in connection with "Preview Commentary". It strikes me that interference has come from the sources I have just enumerated.

The Quebec Conservative members and their political allies, the Union Nationale, are now trying to destroy the C.B.C.; or at least if not, they are trying to prevent it from discharging the most important responsibilities it has to discharge in the province of Quebec. In order to achieve their purpose they resort to public denunciations of the C.B.C. and employees who are not in a position to defend themselves, and in this way they hope to destroy the morale of these officers of the C.B.C. and spread fear amongst the employees, with the hope that, put in that position, they will remove themselves and go off to other spheres.
They may get away temporarily with these unfair tactics. I want to tell them, however, that if they succeed in destroying the C.B.C., either by fear or through lack of funds or by reducing the C.B.C. to a political instrument of the government, they will be responsible for a major blow to the development and progress of the culture which they pretend to be serving and defending. I want to tell them also that in spite of a few mistakes which have been made by the C.B.C., this public service is still strongly and enthusiastically supported by public opinion.
I repeat that we on this side of the house and the Canadian public generally are entitled to get from the government a clear and complete statement of its broadcasting policy. This has not been forthcoming. This has not been given, either in the committee or here by the minister, and I think the time has arrived for the minister to tell this house that he, as the one speaking for the C.B.C., will not for one moment stand for interference, no matter from where it comes, be it from the members from the province of Quebec or elsewhere, in the programming of the C.B.C.
He and his government have repeatedly stated, not only during the dispute in Montreal but earlier on other occasions, that they will not permit interference in the affairs of the C.B.C. Well, if that is the case, then it appears to me that he should give instructions, in the same way instructions were given that "Preview Commentary" be returned to the air, to the C.B.C. to restore "Point de Mire" and other programs which have been taken off. In the present unfortunate circumstances what is needed to restore confidence and morale is an authoritative statement by the government. I sincerely hope that will be forthcoming.
Then, sir, the hon. member for Roberval a moment ago challenged me to put on the record certain statements in connection with what happened in Montreal recently. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Montreal

Star dated July 8, 1959 entitled, "RC Group Presents Views on TV, Radio". I quote:
It is time to stop wholesale condemnation and negative criticism of radio and television productions, Paul Emile Cardinal Leger said yesterday.
That is just the opposite to what the hon. member for Roberval told us in his 25-minute speech. He went on to be critical and to condemn many of the things that were being done by the C.B.C. None the less the head of the church in the province of Quebec did not hesitate to say that it is time to stop wholesale condemnation and negative criticism of radio and television productions.
At the meeting which took place at that time a series of resolutions were passed. I have not time to put them on the record, but they are there for anyone who wants to see them. I conclude, sir, by saying the time has arrived for the government to make it quite clear that there will be no interference in the programs on the French network of the C.B.C. I hope the minister will not only do that but that he will see to it that, in the same way "Preview Commentary" was restored to the air on the English speaking network, "Point de Mire" and other programs which have been dropped in Quebec will be restored to the French network.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to make some extended remarks on this item, because I am very much interested in the C.B.C. and all connected with it. But owing to the desire of the house generally to proceed as expeditiously as possible today I am going to deny myself that treat and enjoyment. However, the hon. member for Port Arthur placed before this house this party's position with respect to the C.B.C., and since coming into the house I have heard from a number of hon. members that his presentation was very well received even by members on the government side of the house, and that it was a constructive contribution to this most important subject.
I am going to deal with one or two matters that are of local interest, but before doing so I must say that I have received many letters-and I know a great number of people in my constituency-in connection with C.B.C. news programs and commentaries. These programs are enjoyed and appreciated by a large section of the population, that is to say that section of the population in my constituency which has the opportunity to enjoy those programs. I may say that included in those programs are excellent commentaries conducted by various members of the press gallery whose names have become almost household words in most of Canada because of their commentaries on radio and television.

However, it is because of the fact that the C.B.C. and its programs are appreciated in a large portion of my constituency that those who are still denied even radio reception are becoming more and more vocal in their protests against this continued denial of radio reception. Here we are spending huge sums of money developing television, yet in Canada today we stiR have sections of this country, such as the northern portion of my constituency where there are about five thousand people at the present time, who are denied the opportunity even to hear Canadian Broadcasting Corporation radio programs.
I have made this protest over a period of 14 years, Mr. Chairman, and we have made some progress. We are pleased to know that low power relay transmitters are going to be established this year at Slocan and New Denver. That is a step in the right direction, and the persons who will be served appreciate it very much. We still have two other areas which are not served by C.B.C. programs and which have extremely unsatisfactory radio reception. The same situation exists with respect to people around the Kootenay lake area. I urge the minister to prod the C.B.C. along in this respect. Oh, oh.
You monopolized most of the time.

I hear the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville say that I monopolized most of the time. I almost raised a question of privilege in the committee because a very distinguished journalist wrote about me that I merely went into the committee for five minutes, obtained headlines and then left. You cannot have it both ways. There was one occasion when it was quite impossible for me to be there. I admit that most of those sittings that were held when the house was in session-and I do not blame anyone for it-took place when I felt it was my duty to be here rather than there. Politics.
-policy and legislation.
Politics.

when a shocking attack was made upon public broadcasting in Canada by the premier of the most populous province of Canada, and I thought the premier of that province should be invited to come to the committee in order to give us his views. Other hon. gentlemen can give their own testimony on this subject. The Leader of the Opposition was critical; but understandably, since he was not a member of the committee, he was relatively mildly critical of the report of the committee and of some of its deliberations. I agree with everything he said, and I should like to reinforce it a little. I want to examine these recommendations seriatim. The first one does not need much time spent on it, as the hon. member for Port Arthur pointed out. It reads as follows:
Your committee affirms its support of the basic aims and objectives of the C.B.C. We commend the officers of the corporation for their efforts to further these aims and objectives.
There it is. There is not another thing in that report that indicates that they are trying to do anything to attain those objectives. From there on the recommendations deal with breaking down the capacity of the C.B.C. to do those things, or with matters irrelevant thereto.
The next recommendation is:
Your committee regrets that it must report its conviction that the administrative structure of the corporation is weak and in need of a thorough revision. There is a lack of clear definition of responsibilities and authority of the various executives and junior executives of the corporation.
I must say that I do not agree at all with that recommendation. I do think there was obvious evidence of weakness at the very top; I do not think anyone could argue that. But for the rest of the officers who appeared, I have very grave doubts as to whether there is any private corporation in this country which could send the number and variety of its officers to be put through the kind of inquisition these witnesses were put through and have them as clear, as candid and as precise about their functions.
It did not seem to me, therefore, that there was any warrant whatsoever for this wholesale suggestion. I think everyone would agree, and it would be silly not to

agree, that for reasons perhaps partly stemming from Mr. Dunton's resignation and then the illness of Mr. Ouimet and the extraordinary burden thrown on Mr. Bushnell, there was weakness at the top; but in the corporation generally I found nothing whatever to warrant this, and of course no concrete evidence is cited in this recommendation.
Then the next recommendation:
Your committee believes that the board must assume full responsibility for policy-
Of course I do not agree with that either. The position of our party, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this morning, is that the policy for broadcasting should be made by the board of broadcast governors for the whole national system, public as well as private, and having a board of directors of the C.B.C. is at best redundant and at worst likely to lead to confusion; and, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out at the last session of parliament, likely to create a divorce between the public and private systems, which would be regrettable.
That does not mean at all that we do not think the private sector of broadcasting- I should have said I do not think-has an important part, and an increasingly important part, to play; but the original conception from 1936 on was that there should be one integrated system with public and private parts complementary, and not two separate systems. It seems to me that already we have had a lot of evidence on this point, including the evidence given by the chairman of the board of broadcast governors, who gave his evidence very precisely and very concisely and who made it very clear that, as things operate now, they have no initiative at all in an effective sense in the field of policy.
Then coupled with this is the recommendation that-
-the person occupying the position of chairman of the board shall not hold other executive offices in the corporation, and that a chairman of the board be appointed.
I have some doubt as to whether the committee had the power to make that recommendation, because we were not asked to recommend changes in legislation; but perhaps that is a pedantic objection. I must say that in default of anything better I think this would be some improvement on the existing situation. It would provide a little of that insulation which the Leader of the Opposition indicated very clearly this morning was lacking and of which we need a lot and not just a little.
I pass over the next recommendation for the moment, because I want to say something about it later. It is the one having to do
Supply-National Revenue with clandestine political influence. The next recommendation I come to is this:
Your committee recommends that a senior officer of the corporation, with headquarters in Ottawa, be vested with the clear authority and responsibility for all supervision of production.
That, and several other recommendations which come later on, struck me as indicating a fundamental weakness in the approach of the majority of this committee to their duties. They seemed to think that this committee was appointed to run the C.B.C. This parliament last year over our objection established a board of directors to run the C.B.C., and this report is filled with administrative directions to that board of directors. The worst feature of that, sir, was that the committee took it upon itself deliberately to usurp the authority of the board of directors.
The Minister of National Revenue came to the committee and reinforced the reasons given by the C.B.C., some of them I admit perhaps not as convincing as they should have been, why certain information of a commercial character should not be given to that committee. Notwithstanding the fact that the minister made a very strong case-I thought it a more convincing case than the C.B.C.'s on this particular point-and notwithstanding the fact that all the opposition members of the committee voted to sustain the position of the minister, the majority of this committee took it upon themselves to disregard his advice and to insist upon asking for this information.
But that is not all; we then have chapter 2. There was a formal meeting of the board of directors, this board of directors which was set up by the whole of parliament, not just this little committee, to carry on the affairs of the C.B.C.; and this board, appointed by this Tory government, a board which one would imagine would not be unfriendly to the government, passed a resolution asking the committee to reconsider this matter. And what happened in the committee? Every supporter of the government voted against what the minister wanted; they voted against what the board appointed by the government wanted, and voted to insist upon overriding parliament. That was the kind of committee we had; and the only members of that committee who voted to uphold what has been, since Mr. Meighen laid down those principles about the C.N.R. in 1919 or 1920, the proper attitude toward the running of a public corporation were the opposition members of the committee.
Now, sir, it seems to me we have to make up our minds one way or the other. Either this parliament is going to show some reasonable confidence in the directors appointed to

Supply-National Revenue manage these corporations, or it is going to get rid of them because it has no confidence in them. The idea that we can usurp their functions and set up committees which disregard the advice of the minister who has to answer is, in my view, the negation of our British system of responsible government. It is importing into our system of government the United States system; and I must say that when I heard the Prime Minister's remarks this morning about the committee system I thought the Prime Minister himself was beginning to get worried. The Prime Minister said, as I remember it-I am just paraphrasing-"We are not trying to introduce the United States system." Whether or not the government is trying to introduce it, certainly many of the members of this committee acted as though that were being done.
The committee then went on to say that they gave lengthy attention to the financial operations of the corporation, and that is not a recommendation. They then went on to say something about extending service. That is one recommendation I do agree with. As rapidly as it reasonably can be done I think service should be extended to all Canadians to whom service can be extended. There is one other sentence with which I agree unreservedly, and it is this:
Your committee was unable to ascertain that there is any intelligible formula or pattern used in determining the annual budget of the C.B.C.
That is exactly what we said about this legislation last year,	and	that is exactlywhat the Leader	of	the	Opposition	saidabout it at page 4053 of Hansard of last year. I wish I had time to read what he said, because it was borne out completely by the evidence which was brought before us on the very first day.	It	was	quite clear	thatwhat we said at	the	last	session of	parliament was true, namely that, as long as they had annual budgets based on no kind of principle except that of asking for as much as they thought they could get, with the Minister of Finance trying to keep the amount as low as possible, it meant that this corporation to all intents and purposes was under the thumb of the Minister of Finance. I am glad the committee recognized at the end of its sessions that what some of us recognized on the very first day was true, but I do not think much of the proposals they have for dealing with the problem.
It seems to me, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out so well this morning, that there is only one way of dealing with this problem, and that is by some means or other, for a reasonable period of years, to permit reasonable planning, to give to the

corporation an assured budget based on some automatic formula that cannot be changed by the Minister of Finance, the treasury board or the governor in council; a formula that will be decided by legislation in this parliament, and which will stand until it is changed by parliament. Before any formula of that sort would be changed I should think it would be wise to do what has always been done in the past, have an investigation of the character of the Fowler or Massey commissions.
These other recommendations about commercialism and the other cases where the committee undertook to tell the board of directors how to run the corporation, I am not going to discuss very much. I think this whole conception of commercialism is entirely wrong. That does not mean that I do not think the corporation should get as much out of the advertisers as it can, because I do; but I think it is entirely wrong to talk about subsidizing advertisers. What the corporation is supposed to do is to give the Canadian people the kind of programs that are needed in the national interests of Canada, and to try to get a part of those programs paid for by commercial interests. I am not the least bit in favour of letting commercial corporations go into the field and run programs in place of the C.B.C.
Well, who is?
I direct the hon. member's attention to the last of the recommendations, which suggested that this should be taken over by sponsors or advertising agencies.
That is a complete misunderstanding of the report.

It may be a complete misunderstanding of the report, but it is an understanding shared by most of those who have read it. I come back to the paragraph in the report which I passed over. I refer to this incredible and extraordinary statement;
Your committee investigated the charge that "clandestine political influence" was responsible for the removal of the program, "Preview Commentary" and found no evidence to support the charge.
Well, we did not find any evidence that did not support the charge; nothing; not a tittle of it. First of all Mr. Bushnell admitted quite frankly that he believed his head would roll unless he did something about that program and did it quickly. He communicated that belief to the senior officers of the corporation. They ended the program in a panic, and then got into a second panic and put it back on the air. We attempted to solve the whodunit, to try to find out what the channel was through which Mr. Bushnell got this impression, which I do not think

was an hallucination on his part, though it might have been. We wanted two further witnesses. The steering committee agreed to have one of those witnesses, but the hearings were terminated abruptly before that witness could be heard. We wanted to have another witness, a member of the board of directors, who according to testimony already given really knew something about this matter, but we were turned down by every member of the majority voting against extending an invitation to those witnesses who might have been able to solve this problem.
Why? I do not know why, but it was evident that there must have been a fear on the part of the members of the majority that the evidence would be very damaging politically.
Ridiculous.

The hon. gentleman can make his own speech in his own time. I want now to make one or two further observations about this whole question. One thing we know is that this program was cancelled suddenly, precipitately, and we were even told that it ought to have been taken off the air a week before it was. Let me read these words:
-the fact is that it was cancelled after it had been announced. Why was it cancelled? Who reached the decision to cancel it ?- On what grounds did they make their decision? With what information before them and with what communications before them did they reach that decision?
I ask the minister that. I continue:
Looking about for the source of this idea to cancel an announced program (an announced series of programs) which to say the least were not always complimentary to (the government), is it not fair to ask this question: Where does the advantage accrue from such a cancellation? To even the most untutored in the tortuous ways of this government it is perfectly obvious that the only advantage that could accrue from the cancellation of that program was an advantage to the (Conservative) party and the government opposite. Hence, Mr. (Chairman) we are left with two alternative explanations.
The first one is that this program must have been cancelled by request of the government. I am not so naive as to suggest that the Prime Minister wrote a letter to Mr. (Bushnell) and asked that this program should be cancelled. Oh, no; I do not make that suggestion. I do not even suggest that the Minister of National Revenue necessarily picked up the telephone and called Mr. (Bushnell) or spoke with anyone representing the (C.B.C. management).
That is sheer nonsense and you know it. Your conduct is befitting a kindergarten.

I agree, Mr. Chairman, that this statement was sheer nonsense when it was uttered by the hon. member for Eglinton on February 7, 1956, as reported at page 947
Supply-National Revenue of Hansard in connection with another incident, but it is not on this occasion. I am interested that the minister should have used the very favourite expression of the hon. member for Eglinton in talking about what he describes as "sheer nonsense". But how well it applies. I am going to read a few more lines, because these words apply so very well to this situation.

There was some
evidence then.

The hon. gentleman can deal with that in his own time. It happens that there was absolutely none. The other alternative explanation is that the (C.B.C. management), in proceeding to cancel this program, was acting in the interests of the government and the (Conservative) party even without direct government intervention.
Sir, of the two alternatives the second would be the worst for Canada because it would mean that- the responsible body in the Canadian broadcasting organization, was anticipating government desires in tihs matter and was showing such a tender solicitude for the partisan interests of the government as would serve the desires of the government. Take your choice, Mr. (Chairman), of those two alternative explanations.
Suspicion could not fail to be aroused by the method in which this matter has been handled- There was no frank, straightforward statement coming from them.
We remember the answer the Prime Minister gave on June 24. I advise hon. members to refresh their memories by looking at it. I continue with the hon. member for Eglinton in 1956:
No, it is quite obvious that they felt they had something to hide; they had something to hold back and therefore the (intervention) must be secret.
The Minister of Finance anticipated the kind of situation that would exist with a Tory government in office very accurately indeed, as will be seen from the reading of that passage. But he was not the only one who anticipated that. That is precisely what was said by the Leader of the Opposition in the

Supply-National Revenue reference I made a few moments ago to Hansard of last year. That was also said by several hon. members on this side. I could read other extracts to that effect. I do not want to take the time of the committee to do it.
I think the Minister of Finance was right in this, that the greater of the two dangers in this business of voting annual appropriations, the more serious one, is the insensibly, inevitably, because of the corporation's desire to retain its employees, to preserve its status and to continue to grow, if this system of annual appropriations under the thumb of the Minster of Finance is long continued, human nature being what it is, the corporation will try to please, try to ingratiate, try to make sure, particularly in the autumn when treasury board is going to be looking into these matters-and we were given evidence that treasury board did look into them, that there was no question as there is with the C.N.R. of a budget, but there was a fairly detailed examination-we will find that this will insensibly happen, probably for a little while, anyway, for a few months. That may be a greater danger than the danger of direct intervention because of displeasure, perhaps because the government, having had its fingers burned rather badly, may be more cautious for a little while. The whole system is pernicious; it is thoroughly unsound, and it seems to me, sir, we ought to go back to first principles here.
The United States view is that broadcasting is so dangerous-that is, domestic broadcasting within their own country-that the state should not be engaged in it; that it is a danger to freedom. Now, to some degree that is right; to some degree it is true that there is always a danger within a mechanism owned by the state. No matter how great the independence that is given to it, it may become an instrument of the government in office and be a potential danger to our system of free and democratic government, to that proper balance between the government and the opposition which is so essential to the preservation of that freedom. But we have recognized in Canada that if we are to have a national identity side by side with a country so much more powerful than ours we have to have an instrument like this, just as we had to have a transcontinental railway nearly a century ago for the same reason.
Perhaps this is even more essential than the railway was to our preservation, but the only way we can do that is to keep this mechanism divorced as completely as possible, compatible with the parliamentary control over expenditures. That does not mean, sir, that you have to have parliamentary

control over the day to day expenditures, and you certainly should not have governmental or treasury board control over them.
My view is-and I feel it even more strongly than I did before-that treasury board control is wrong; that the right system is some kind of ceiling, some kind of automatic one. I do not think, if it is properly calculated, we will need to worry very much about what happens below it because the corporation, as everyone with a limited income will have to choose what is best within that ceiling on income.

I know there is a divergence of opinion in that regard, but that is one yardstick we can use, and it is surprising the number of letters one gets to that effect.
Much has been said this afternoon about the committee report. I am not here to make any defence of the committee. I do not think defence is necessary. I was very glad to hear the tributes paid by some members to the chairman of that committee. They

were well deserved. I think the same tribute can also be paid to the great majority of the committee members. The committee worked hard and sat long hours. I think it did a remarkably good job.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate protested because the committee brought in certain recommendations, and said it was unfair to the management of the C.B.C. Maybe that is a play on words, inasmuch as the recommendations have to do with matters involving management. I can remember a score of committees of the house that have brought in recommendations with respect to specific matters. They are not necessarily binding on the government, but are the opinion of groups of men and women who have sat for long hours, have heard witnesses and have arrived at certain conclusions by a process of discussion and sometimes, of course, by long discussion and modifications before something approaching unanimity was reached.
The report is a good one. I do not know how far the corporation will be prepared to go in carrying out the recommendations of the committee. I am not sure what if any recommendations involve government action. This is something to which the government will give consideration when time permits after the pressures of these immediate days are over.
Much has been said about this program "Preview Commentary". I am not going to rethrash that old straw again. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is sometimes logical and always political and has a habit of raising his voice higher the weaker his case, this time spoke more loudly than I have ever heard him before. I never heard him make such a poor presentation. I understand he is studying law, and I thought that undoubtedly some day he would be an ornament to the bar of whatever province he chose to join.
This afternoon, when he talked about evidence, I realized he had a long way to go before he became a lawyer. We all know there are books that have to be read during the law course, and if one wants to learn about evidence one of the elementary books one has to read is called "Phipson on Evidence". There are many other books on evidence, and I suggest to the hon. member that he should read a book or two on evidence before he starts trying to describe to the House of Commons or anyone else what evidence may or may not be.
Is a parliamentary committee a court?

No, a parliamentary committee is not a court. However, one often hears a

Supply-National Revenue reference to the high court of parliament, so one is left to draw one's own conclusions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do the rules of evidence apply in a committee?
The rules of evidence may not apply, but when the hon. member speaks about something being proven, and when he says that things are proven, it leaves the impression that he is referring to evidence.
I know the minister does not want to misrepresent what I said, but I did not use the word "prove" anywhere.

The hon. member did not use the word, but he made references to this evidence and one draws an inference from that. Apparently there is some suggestion of political interference and some suggestion that political pressure was brought to bear in connection with this program. Well, I have heard this government described in various rough terms by hon. members on the other side of the house, as having failed in this and failed in that and failed in the other thing. I believe most of these charges are not correct. However, I have never heard any description of this government or of any member of the government that was so uncomplimentary as to suggest that if there was any desire or any intention to use political pressure to cancel this program, it would have been done in such a way and at such a time. Certainly no politician with a scintilla or a modicum of intelligence would have done it in that way.
I think that is the best answer. How could anyone suggest that if political pressures were to be used to cancel this program, they would be used when this house was going to close within a week or two, after sitting months and months, and the program having gone on for two years? To do it in such a fashion would be utter nonsense. Just how silly can they get over there? They even have to laugh themselves.
Of course when they make such suggestions they know how little foundation there can be. The program may have been cancelled ineptly and without proper discussion. One can admit in a moment that is a matter for management as to why it was done or how it was done, and in that way management must answer for it. However, I can give assurance, as I have done before in the house and in the committee, that the suggestion that it was done by political pressure, clandestine or otherwise, influence or pressure, is sheer nonsense in every way, shape and form.
The hon. member for Laurier, who usually is very logical and makes able and convincing speeches in this house, I thought was

Supply-National Revenue driven to rather unfair limits when he suggested there were questions which should be put and answered. I suggest there may be theoretical questions about everything under the sun. If everyone goes around trying to make up questions and give answers about everything from creation to the hereafter, they will be rather busy indeed.
The hon. member referred to some question about the role of the Prime Minister and the role of someone else. I have been actively associated, as Minister of National Revenue, with this corporation from the day we took office on June 21, 1957. I have been the only one who has been associated with it in any way, shape or form. For anyone to suggest that the Prime Minister, directly or indirectly, interfered with this corporation through me or through anyone else is absolutely untrue and unwarranted; there can be no question on that score whatever.
Much has been said about the budget and the fact that the poor C.B.C. is defenceless because the government, through parliament, prescribes the moneys which the corporation is to receive. Well, what was the situation when we came into office? Where was this formula about which we hear so much now? I will tell you what the situation was. When we came into office the government of the day, represented by some hon. members who have been speaking this afternoon, had only provided the C.B.C. with enough money to keep it operating until October. In order to be fair I should say there was a royal commission and they were awaiting the royal commission report, but the royal commission report was not going to provide the money, per se. You had to go to parliament.
The first thing I had to do, as Minister of National Revenue, was to get a supplementary estimate through this house to keep the corporation from closing down. Something was said, and I think there is a misunderstanding about this-with all due respect I think the hon. member for Port Arthur has a misunderstanding of it because some of his questions would imply this- about my responsibility with respect to money. Not only am I the minister who reports to parliament or who is responsible for reporting to parliament for the C.B.C., but under the act I also have to recommend to cabinet every expenditure which has to come before the cabinet. What was the situation when I took office? I found that the minister responsible for the C.B.C. had to recommend to cabinet every expenditure over $25,000.
Is the minister not just referring to capital expenditures?

No; for any expenditure over $25,000, under the C.B.C. act the corporation had to get the authorization of the governor in council. Of course this would imply, as I am sure the hon. member will agree, a recommendation by the minister, whoever he might be, to council to get that authorization through. When we drafted this new bill which has been criticized-I am certainly not suggesting for one minute it is a perfect piece of legislation; I said that last year and I say it again-what we did do was to raise that ceiling from $25,000 to $100,000, and we eliminated programming entirely from that consideration.
Under the old act and under the former government, everything over $25,000 for programming had to be approved by the governor in council. Under the present act expenditures over $100,000 have to be approved by the governor in council, but programming is not included. I happen to know of one expenditure for programming that is going to cost $1 million which does not have to have my recommendation or my approval in any way, shape or form. This is a long term program, running over three or four years, but I happen to know about it.
I do not believe there is any basis whatever for this charge that the corporation is under the control of the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue and is weakened in any way because parliament has to vote the money. There is such a difference in the last four or five years. The cocoon has blossomed forth. The days are over when the C.B.C. budget was $4 million or $5 million. Radio was a constant factor, and expansion had ceased. The experimental era was pretty well over. You could plan a budget for a certain period.
We have blossomed forth from a budget of $7 million or $10 million to $60 million in a period of four or five years. What formula could you adopt to cover an expanding situation such as that, I should like to know?
What was the situation when my hon. friends opposite were in power? They had a formula at one time. At one time they had licence fees plus advertising revenues and you had to live within that formula or you had to fire someone. At one time they had a budget and licence fees, and it was not sufficient to run the corporation. Gradually they outgrew the licence fee; there were difficulties of collecting it, and they got a fixed parliamentary grant of $7,500,000 a year for the last three years, I think it was.
Then there was the excise tax. They had no reasonable formula whatsoever; I refer to hon. members on the other side of the house. It is true that the excise tax provided a new

source of income, but when the corporation needed less money, compared at least with later years, the amount that came to them was larger because everybody was buying a television set and therefore the excise tax was larger and was far beyond their needs. And when the corporation needed money most less was coming in because people had bought their television sets.
To say they had a formula is a play on words. What our predecessors in office were doing-and what I suggest they would be doing today, or what they were doing up until the day we took over-was voting money by parliament. They had a parliamentary grant. They had the excise tax. They also voted money for the last year's grant and for the last two years we voted money for a deficit just as we are doing now. The only difference is that the deficit is bigger now than it was then.
Will the minister permit a question at this point?
Yes.

Is that not precisely the reason that was given here in this house by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance for the appointment of a royal commission, namely that we believed this was a bad system and we wanted a royal commission to recommend a better one?
I am not prepared to answer that question; I may say quite frankly that I have not read Hansard. I have not any doubt that the hon. member is giving his recollection and that he probably is correct.
It is a fact.

I am trying to suggest only that there is no difference in our procedure in this matter today from the procedure carried on by the hon. members opposite. Maybe we are low on this; maybe there should be more. But I do suggest that in this expensive area you cannot adopt a formula which will be satisfactory at this time. Theoretically it is fine. When the situation stabilizes I think a formula should be and could be found. But I say that in my opinion and that of my colleagues

because this matter was discussed; the Fowler commission undoubtedly recommended a formula-we did not believe and I do not believe that it is a practical suggestion. Therefore we have not adopted it. When you are dealing with $50 million, $60 million, and $70 million a year coming from the taxpayers of the country I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that some form of parliamentary control and parliamentary vote is highly desirable as a protection to the C.B.C. itself, because there are bound to be these pressures arise and there
Supply-National Revenue are bound to be demands from people across the country to know how the money is being spent. Even if you had a formula within which they could operate, I doubt that you would find that it could be preserved in our modern parliamentary practice as it is carried on.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, there are many matters to which I should like to refer. I thought the hon. member for Port Arthur was somewhat critical of the board of broadcast governors and the chairman who, I think, was before the committee twice. However, I think there is a misunderstanding in his mind as to the role of the broadcast governors with respect to the C.B.C. The board of broadcast governors never was intended to have any control over the C.B.C. with regard to programming or anything of that kind. The board of broadcast governors is to lay down general rules and principles for the operation of all radio and television stations in Canada, both public and private. It has no more relationship to the C.B.C., except that it happens to be a government agency and is here in Ottawa, than it would have to a private radio station such as that to which my hon. friend referred in Port Arthur, or to a radio station in Calgary or wherever it may be.
Reports all over this country from persons in the private broadcasting business as well as the public generally are that the board of broadcasting governors have made a remarkable impression, and are doing a remarkably good job and have received commendation from all over the country. I think we are very happy indeed in this government and in this parliament, and that this country is fortunate, in having a man of the type of Dr. Stewart and the other men who are associated with him in the administration and control of licensing of radio and television broadcasting throughout this country. It is because of that fact that the government has announced the relaxation of policy, because I feel confident that we can turn over to the board of broadcast governors the responsibility of deciding where and when and who shall be getting these television licences and know that the very best decision that can be made by human beings subject to human error will be made.
My friend the hon. member for Laurier referred to a certain program. I thought there was a slight lack of logic there. We are accused of political influence or clandestine political influence in connection with the program "Preview Commentary". Yet apparently he was suggesting there should be some overt political interference in order to

Supply-National Revenue get a certain program-I did not catch the name of it-which he wanted restored to the French network.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. I do not want to interrupt the minister, but I am sure he does not want to misrepresent what I said. I thought I made it quite clear, both in the remarks I made in English as well as those I made in French, that if this program "Point de Mire" was withdrawn because of political intereference it should be restored.

Frankly I may say I had
never heard of it being withdrawn until the hon. member raised the matter this morning.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is withdrawn.

I can tell you without any hesitation whatsoever, because I have been so advised by the officials, that the decision to withdraw that program was taken many months ago, and that it was done by the corporation without any suggestion of political interference whatsoever; and the program is not going to be restored in the near future. It is a program that some day may be brought back, but that is a decision of management and the decision will be made purely by them. As I say, frankly I did not know anything about it until I heard the matter raised here this morning.
There are many other matters to which one could refer, but I think I have taken up enough time of the committee at this time. As I said earlier, the C.B.C. has had a very tough season. It has been open season on the C.B.C. Everyone has taken a pot shot at it on the wing or in the bush. Apparently every newspaper felt free to do so, as is its right, as did many individuals. I sometimes wonder whether the advertising dollar and the division of it may not influence to some extent the not entirely friendly criticism which sometimes comes from the press. After all, their share of the advertising dollar will be smaller because as additional stations are licensed there will be greater competition. But as I said at the beginning and say again, I want to pay my tribute to the men and women of the C.B.C. who through very difficult days for the most part-with some exceptions-have been loyal to the corporation and have done a remarkably good job. I emphasize again loyalty to the corporation, because this corporation must exist as a corporation and those who are associated with it must have pride in it and show their loyalty to it. I am sure of that being done.
It has been a most unfortunate occurrence that Mr. Ouimet has had a long and serious illness, but we are all glad to hear that-at

least according to the present advice of his doctors-he will soon be able to return to his office. In fact he intends to return to his office some time in August. Mr. Bushnell wore himself out in the interests of this corporation and worked harder for it than any other man I know. After a short rest I hope he will come back. I am confident that this corporation will continue to make in future the contribution to Canada which it has made in the past.
Someone has referred critically to the committee because in its report it referred to matters of administration. I think it was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Although I am not in a position to judge, I do know that most editorial comment in Canada-I said editorial comment; I am not quite sure whether it was biased-agreed with the criticism of the administrative weaknesses in the C.B.C.
Would the minister permit me to say that I said there was no evidence produced before the committee. I direct his attention to the word "evidence".

Well, whatever the administrative weaknesses are, I am glad to see that the directors and the executive committee have taken cognizance of them, and I hope that whoever is responsible for piloting these estimates through the committee a year from now will find that next year has been a more stable year than the past year and that these difficulties have been resolved.

May I express the hope that a year from now the minister will still be piloting these estimates, through the commons. However, in order not to have any misunderstanding about the position, a misunderstanding which might be left in view of what the minister has said, may I make it quite clear that when we support a formula for income for the C.B.C. we do not mean a formula which would prejudice parliamentary control of expenditure in any way. We mean by a formula the kind of thing which was recommended by the report of the Fowler commission, which was set up by the previous government and which was the reason no action was taken earlier; a commission which recommended three types of formulae to deal with the changing situation in broadcasting.

I will be very glad to draw that matter to the attention of the corporation. I am afraid I hafe not here the names of the personnel of the religious council to which the hon. member referred. There are one or two officers in the programming department who, in consultation with the the religious council, lay down religious programming.

I wonder if the minister has any information from his officials about the cancellation of a drama from Winnipeg dealing with a political topic, which program has been either deferred or cancelled because of its nature?
I heard a rumour to that effect last night. I have checked with my officials, and they know nothing about it.
My second question, Mr. Chairman, is this. Can the minister tell us whether he is going to continue to try to get himself relieved of this particular part of his responsibilities?
That depends. If pressures of work keep on increasing in the Department of National Revenue as well as this department, I may just have to be relieved of something because I cannot carry it.

If the minister does push that in this way he might be able, by following the proceedings in the House of Commons committee on broadcasting, to discover that there were one or two members of his party who seemed to have a real national conception as to what the C.B.C. has to do, and those members might very well be worth recommending to take over this chore that the minister wants to get rid of.

I can tell the hon. member that out of the 211 Conservative members of the House of Commons at least 200 would have the same idea of the service of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that he
Supply-National Revenue has, and the hon. member has no monopoly of affection for the C.B.C., or of desire to serve.

Item agreed to.
44. Grant for the capital requirements, including the replacement of existing capital assets, of the radio and television services, $9,197,000.

I would like to ask the minister if the corporation has given consideration at any time during the present calendar year to the acquisition of a television studio in Montreal, by means of an arrangement to have it built for them and leased to them, and if he could give some details about it?

I have not the details here, Mr. Chairman. The corporation was apparently giving consideration to the construction or acquisition of a building in Montreal to which I referred before the committee the other day. This matter came before me in the regular way as the minister who had to sign the recommendation because it involved an expenditure of over $100,000. I questioned that expenditure, as is now the policy-that was the first time I did so, because apparently I had overlooked it-and I said that I was not recommending any more expenditures unless they were approved by the board of directors. It does not necessarily follow that if I recommended it to the board they would approve it, though I should hope they would. I intended to ask about that matter yesterday, but I forgot to bring the papers down with me. The matter was referred to Mr. Dunsmore, the chairman of the finance committee of the board, but to date I have not heard any further.
Might I ask the minister if it is the opinion of the corporation that such a building for a television studio is required in Montreal?
I know the board has been giving consideration to it and there have been discussions with management and the directors, but I am not sure what decision has been arrived at.

Has the minister been advised that there was a definite letter of intent signed by the president of the corporation to a certain corporation in Montreal authorizing them to go ahead with this project subject to approval by the governor in council?
I was advised, or rather I read that in a letter which I received from a member of the House of Commons who pointed it out to me. I have not been advised in any other way, although I inquired a
Supply-National Revenue moment ago and was told that such a letter of intent was sent; but it was stated that it would, of course, be subject to the approval of the governor in council.

Is the minister aware
whether it is the custom for letters of that sort to be sent and to be acted upon on other occasions?
I understand it was the standard wording, the letter which was sent out.

Does the minister think it is a very wise practice, in view of the requirement that the governor in council must approve, for the president of the corporation to make commitments which would to the average businessman, I think, create the impression that he could go ahead? Otherwise it would not appear to have much point at all.

I do not know whether my opinion is very important on this matter, Mr. Chairman. Normally I think he would not send out such a letter unless he were assured it would at least be approved by the board of directors.

In view of the fact that such a letter was sent and, as I am informed, very considerable commitments were made on that account, would the minister feel or would he not feel that some account should be taken of those circumstances if for example two propositions were before the board which were otherwise of equal or virtually equal acceptability?
I would hope that the board would give it very careful consideration.

Quite. Would the minister, the circumstances having been drawn to his attention-I prefer not to mention the name unless the minister wants me to-give an undertaking that if a recommendation to erect a building for television studios comes before him he will look into those circumstances I have mentioned? Will the minister give us that assurance.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
Could the minister tell the committee whether a site has been chosen for the new C.B.C. central office in Toronto, and what plans have been made for constructing a new broadcasting centre there?

No decision has been made as to the location. Officers of the corporation have been looking over properties within the last two weeks. The matter is now under close study to the end that a decision may be reached.

In the committee we heard evidence from the director of engineering to the effect that there will be nine television relay stations or extensions or satellites and some 20 low power relay stations constructed. The request I wish to make to the minister, to pass on to his officials, is that information of this kind be distributed as soon as possible. In many parts of the country it is important that this information be made available as soon as possible in terms of private arrangements that may be under consideration. I would like to ask the minister if he can ascertain from the officials now before him what will be the earliest we can hope that this information will become public knowledge.

I do*not know, Mr. Chairman. I am not at all certain that some of this information should become public knowledge. These are matters for study and consideration. The corporation would have to give careful consideration to these questions.

I suggest it should become public knowledge, because a number of communities in this country have to consider whether or not to make what in many cases are inordinate expenditures in order to prepare for these radio or television facilities. If the C.B.C. has a five-year program, within the limits of population change it should be able to spell out these projected television stations and low power relay stations and state where they will be located. I understood from the reports we had that this information would be available at some time, and I should like to know at what time.
I have no idea, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister is not falling into the egregious error that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources did the other day, and suggesting that information about these extensions should be kept secret.

Oh, no, Mr. Chairman, I did not mean that. I intended to suggest that until decisions are made it would be unwise to have this information become public knowledge. I understand that the matter is under study. Many factors enter into it in terms of population and other things, and only a limited number can be built in any one year. I meant to suggest that until a decision had been made it would be unwise to give publicity to these things. I understand that a decision will be arrived at within the next five or six months.
Mr. Chairman, 1 trust the minister will not consider it necessary to telephone the premier of Ontario to get permission to make an announcement.
Item agreed to.
