speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as the committee know there are a number of items which are of particular interest to those of us who sit on this side of the chamber. While I know it has been the custom to allow most of these items to go through unchallenged-and I would reassure Mr. Speaker at once that it is not my intention to oppose any of them-there is a matter about which we are somewhat concerned on this side. It has to do with the secretaries normally assigned to some of us during the non-sessional period. Before I launch into any discussion of our position with respect to that, I wonder if Mr. Speaker would be so good as to tell the committee what he has in mind in connection with that situation as far as we are concerned.

Before the Speaker does so I wonder if he could give us a report on the results of the investigation he had carried out by the officials of the civil service commission on the more general topic of secretaries and the facilities offered to members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps I could make both those observations together. First may I say the pool system of secretarial assistance for members of the House of Commons has gradually altered in character over the years. We have come to a system whereby all the secretaries are now assigned to the service of individual members. That is a basic change in the former method of operation.
As hon. members will see, the vote for secretarial assistants provides for five secretaries who are called permanent and who are actually civil service appointees. It provides for 33 full time and for 140 sessional employees. The complement at present is in excess of that number both in so-called full time and in sessional secretaries.
In an effort to meet the requirements of the members for more and better secretarial services we went beyond the estimate and have had authorization for the sessional part of that increase. We have today a total of 192 secretaries of all three categories serving
Supply-Legislation
members of the house. Of this number approximately 50 were continued in service during the last recess. That was in excess of the authorized vote. It was warranted perhaps by the fact that the last session continued on into September. There was a shorter interval for holidays, and additional secretarial staff was taken on during that recess to give the full holidays that were due to the secretarial staff. In any event we went beyond our authorized numbers.
The problem I was faced with as this recess approached was to keep within the vote which hon. members have before them, because it was obviously not proper procedure to have on the staff more than the House of Commons authorizes to be paid.
In consultation with all three parties we agreed on a quota basis for each party based on the number of members to be served, and divided the 33 full time positions among the parties, making allowance for some special cases. The agreement was that there would be 24 for the government side, 9 for the Liberal party and 1 for the C.C.F., plus 2 for the office of the leader of the C.C.F. It was my arrangement with the whips that they were to indicate which of the secretaries on the staff would be required during the recess, having regard to the members they were to serve.
That is the basis on which the problem has been met. It obviously means some changes among people who were previously continuous, and it means also the addition of people to the continuous staff who were not formerly continuous, and an adjustment is being made as best can be done within the limits of the funds available.
This is a continuing problem. As all members know, this session we instituted a study not only of the best secretarial arrangement which could be devised to suit our particular needs in the House of Commons, having regard to the recess and members' requirements during recess, but also of the other office arrangements, and that report has been received and is quite interesting. It points in the direction that I have favoured myself, that is reaching the point where we will have a secretary for every member of the house. But we have not reached that stage yet, nor have we enough accommodation; but that I think is the indicated need at the present time having regard to the responsibilities of members.
I should like to read one paragraph of the recommendation which to me affords a reasonable solution in the future of this question with which all members have been concerned. This is the report of the survey of the secretarial services and office facilities of the

Supply-Legislation
house provided by the organization and methods service of the civil service commission. It is dated June 1959, and I am reading from the summary of conclusions on page 37, as follows:
That the plan to provide supervised, small groups of stenographers in offices located close to the members served, and restricted to individual political parties, would be the most effective secretarial system for the House of Commons, and that such a service should include provision for telephone answering, dictation equipment, and allied services.
That confirms the view that many people have expressed that the pool system is antiquated, and that it is desirable now to move to a system for an individual secretarial service close at hand and so arranged that the secretary, when the member is out or when the member is there, can be in a local pool, so to speak, and have facilities for answering the telephone and giving that service as well as acting as a secretary. I think that generally covers the point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the committee will be grateful to His Honour the Speaker for the statement he has just given and also for the position as outlined in the survey concerning future secretarial assistance for members of the House of Commons.
There are one or two observations which come to my mind. The first is this. I wonder whether the Speaker would not give consideration to letting the members of the house see the survey from which he has read. I do not mean that it should be a part of the record of Hansard, but I think all hon. members would be interested in getting a copy of the survey. Perhaps it could be mimeographed and circulated, if His Honour thinks that would be proper.
Now let me deal with the other matter to which His Honour referred, namely the meeting which was held by the various groups in order to arrive at a decision that would apply during the non-sessional period. I believe that what the Speaker indicated on the whole is the agreement that was arrived at, but there is one thing as it affects this side of the house which I would like to bring to his attention, and I wonder whether he would give it a little more active consideration. It is this. Following the election of 1957, there was an agreement that the eight members of the former government were entitled, or would be entitled, to a secretary, whom they would take from the offices which they then vacated, the intention being that the secretaries who had been employed in the various departments of the former ministers should be assigned to them in the opposition with a salary to be fixed by the house.

That was confirmed by agreement. It was contained in correspondence between my hon. friend the member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the Prime Minister. That arrangement has been carried out with but one exception. While I am not free to mention names, and it would be my last intention so to do, I think His Honour knows what I have in mind. There is that unfortunate position in so far as we on this side of the house are concerned. I wonder whether the Speaker would be good enough to take another look at that situation, because we feel that here is a person who left permanent employment at a fixed salary and came over with a former privy councillor to the opposition side of the house. Now that person is going to be without employment during the recess unless the Speaker is good enough to see that she is assigned to someone during the recess.
Having said that, there are just one or two other matters that I would ask the Speaker to give consideration to, and they are these. I know-I am sure-that during the course of the recess it is impossible for the Speaker and those responsible with him for this work to find employment for all the secretaries and stenographers who were taken on during the sessional period, but there are some cases which frankly are pretty serious and are of an emergency nature. I have before me here a number of such cases. I would not like to do other than mention them in a very general way because otherwise they could be identified, and I am sure that is the last thing the committee and the Speaker would want me to do in the circumstances. But I would like to bring to his attention the fact that I know of several cases where these stenographers have reached an age where it is not possible for them to find employment during the recess.
Furthermore, I know that all these cases that have been brought to my attention but one are in this position; that if they are not given employment during the recess period they will be in a pitiful position in so far as, first, their children are concerned; second, their mothers are concerned; and, third, their personal livelihood. Having said that, I know I have said enough so that the Speaker realizes what is in my mind.
Knowing, too, the disposition that the Speaker has made in cases such as these, the very sympathetic manner in which he has approached this whole problem from the beginning, I am sure he will want to give it careful consideration. I ask him on behalf of those who have received representations from this side to take another look at this case of the individual who thought she would have permanent employment when she left a

government department. Then there are several cases, which unfortunately I cannot identify, of stenographers who will suffer seriously if they are left without employment, particularly when there is no notice given to them that their services are about to end.
I understand from the Speaker that there is a 30-day notice in most cases. I know of one case where there has been no such notice, and where it has been indicated that she will have to vacate her position the moment the session is prorogued.
I would draw this final point to the attention of the Speaker. In the United States congress, with which I am sure he is as familiar as most of us, if not more so, the situation is not at all similar to the one here. While I know there are difficulties, it seems to me that no one should be allowed to suffer if that can be avoided. I leave the matter in the hands of the Speaker, content and satisfied that he will want to give it his most careful and sympathetic consideration.

There is one very brief comment I should like to make arising out of the remarks of the Speaker. I will relieve his mind at once by saying that it is not by way of criticism at all but merely to make a suggestion which I hope will be helpful in dealing with what of necessity is a difficult and delicate problem which must have caused him real concern. It has to do with his statement as to the apportionment of the secretaries among the parties.
There is within that problem a regional problem, and a mere apportionment in the way he described to the committee is capable of being somewhat misleading. Bearing in mind the regional problem that exists in the immediate Ottawa area, and bearing in mind the proportion of members of one party or another within that region at any given time, it could put the balance out of line unless that factor is recognized when arriving at a figure as among the parties. If hon. members will consider the regional representation over the last year, when it has been four to one, they will see how that can distort the results. I put this forward with the intention of it being a helpful suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my colleagues I want to express my appreciation for the consideration the Speaker has given to our representations, complaints and requests for adjustments throughout this session. While naturally the Speaker could not always comply with our many requests or correct all our complaints we appreciate
Supply-Legislation
everything he has done to try to make our secretarial and staff work as efficient as possible.
I might say before proceeding that I want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier with respect to those members of the staff who find themselves in difficulties at the end of the session as far as employment is concerned, largely on account of age and so on. I listened with interest to the report the Speaker gave with respect to his survey. I was very interested to hear him speak of working toward the objective of each member having his or her own secretary. I think that is very necessary. Indeed, I look forward to the time when each member will have his or her own office and secretary. In my opinion that is the only way we will have efficient functioning of the secretarial activities in this building. I can readily see from the Speaker's report on the survey and his remarks that he has given serious consideration to improving the efficiency of the secretarial work and staff as far as the House of Commons is concerned.
Before I sit down I must express the appreciation of my colleagues for the devoted service of the staff in this building, the protective staff, the public works staff, the secretarial staff and the cleaning staff. I might say that I often meet the ladies of the cleaning staff when I get here about 7.30 in the morning. The hon. member for Ottawa West is accusing me of something of which I could not possibly be guilty. I hear the various complaints of these ladies, and in that respect I suggest that some consideration might be given to changing their hour of arrival, because apparently they have to arrive half an hour or an hour earlier than is necessary to complete their work in the building before the members arrive. I must not forget the nurse who has treated me very satisfactorily on several occasions during the session for minor ailments, and also some of my colleagues as well.
Before leaving that point, I do want to say that we appreciate the work of the Hansard staff, which is particularly trying under these circumstances and has been during the last month. They are kept here for long hours at a type of work that requires concentration and application, which is very tiring indeed. I think we should recognize the good work they do. I remember being told two or three years ago that the Hansard amanuenses do not get any overtime, and that on one occasion the house prorogued at noon on Saturday and they were paid until noon on Saturday, after working until 11 and 12 o'clock several nights prior to prorogation. I hope the Speaker will be more generous in that respect should such a situation arise this session.

S upp ly-Legis lation
Before concluding I do want to suggest that we have to give some consideration to planning our sessions to better advantage. The way our sessions are handled at the present time is most inconvenient for the majority of the members. There may be a few gentlemen of the legal profession who find it more satisfactory, but I do not see why a dozen or so of these gentlemen should influence the handling of the sessions of the house. There are a lot of farmers here and many other people who have to get out and earn their living. I suggest that we should give some consideration to having our sessions commence on October 15, continue until December 15 and adjourn until January 15 with the aim of proroguing around June 15. In that way we could do our work much more efficiently, plan it to better advantage, and leave the summer months for visiting our constituents and things of that sort.
I have one more thought I wish to express before I sit down. We all know the anxiety to conclude this session today. That is one reason I am denying myself the opportunity to speak on a number of things on which I should like to have spoken, as other members are also doing. But I think we could do a great deal toward a better ending for our session if the whips of all parties would get together a month before the end of the session and commence doing then what we have been doing in the last three days. I think that would make for a much more satisfactory conclusion. We would then all know when we would likely be able to leave, and we could make our reservations.

Mr. Chairman, before the Speaker replies I should like to say a word about one precise point made by the hon. member for Laurier. As he indicated I, at Mr. St. Laurent's direction, wrote a letter about this situation to the Prime Minister on the last day he was leader of the opposition. There was one aspect of the letter that may not have been as explicit as it should have been, but that was followed by certain conversations with the Speaker's predecessor and with an official designated by the Prime Minister to deal with the matter.
There was a very clear understanding that the eight secretaries who came here would be not permanent but on the continuing staff, and that treasury board would increase the appropriation temporarily for that purpose and let it run down again as others retired. It would be, I think, very embarrassing-I do not want to use any extravagant language -if any of these eight persons, so long as they give satisfactory service, of course, was

prejudiced because they could have had positions in the public service of a continuing nature.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I take it this is probably the only general discussion there will be. 1 should like to thank hon. members, not only for the kind things they have said, but for the constructive suggestions that they have made. It would be of interest to discuss some of these problems at greater length, but this is not the stage of the session to do so. I am glad hon. members take the opportunity of coming to me with these administrative problems during the session, and I hope most of them can be settled and dealt with in that way. We, unfortunately, have to work within the limits of the estimates which are before us. I appreciate particularly the problems which have been mentioned of the sessional and continuous stenographic staff. I have been personally much concerned about them and I am concerned about them now. I believe hon. members will find the arrangements which are being made satisfactory.
It was, perhaps, an excess of amiability which got us into trouble last year in making the arrangements to which the hon. member has referred for the service of former ministers, of local members, and in meeting the reasonable requirements of the members for assistance during the recess. In this way we got our recess staff 12 above the number which was provided for in the vote. I am hopeful that this problem is a temporary one. The report which has been made, I think, points the way to improvement. I shall be glad to have this report circulated. I am indebted to all hon. members who assisted in the investigation and who wrote letters giving their views. They point clearly to one course, an individual office and an individual stenographer for every member of the house. So far as I am concerned, that is the direction in which we should go and the direction in which I am going in so far as I have to do with it. As I say, we have at this moment to work within the estimates before us and I shall do the best I can within those limits to meet the problems which have been pointed out.
I should like to add a word of appreciation to the staff here. We are well served in this house by our temporary and our permanent staff, sometimes under conditions which we find trying ourselves and I am sure must be even more trying for others. If there are other points to be raised, I shall be glad to consider them.

The comments I have to make would more properly come under items 182 and 183, but I understand this is a sort of

general discussion period, so I shall make them now. Apparently one of the almost universal questions that is asked, especially by visitors who come here not only from Canada but other countries, relates to the young gentlemen who are our page boys. I have wondered about it for some time, as I am sure other members have. I think it might be most enlightening, certainly to some members of the house and to the general public, if Mr. Speaker were able to relate some of the educational facilities for our staff of young gentlemen who are our page boys, so far as their formal education is concerned.
I would suggest one other thing for consideration of His Honour, if I may. I refer to the difference in salary structure between the protective staff and the messenger staff. If one looks at the items listed in the detailed section of the blue book, one sees that the difference in salary structure ranges somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1,000 a year. I would suggest this might be a matter for consideration, the bringing of the salary structure of the messenger staff more closely in line with that of the protective staff. The question of responsibility is not the one on which we should make a comparison. In so far as work is concerned, the moving about of equipment and things of that nature, the messenger staff performs a prime function in connection with the efficient operation of the house. May I suggest that might be one question taken into consideration, to bring the messenger staff salary structure more closely in line with that of the protective service.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would just say one word about the page boys. All hon. members know that these young lads who serve us here cannot avoid having their formal education interfered with as a result of the service which they give here for remuneration. I am hopeful that they learn other things here which will stand them in good stead in the future. I have a complete report on our page staff for the present session and I find that all of them are reasonably well advanced in their school year, having regard to their school age, so we are assured to some extent that we are not robbing them of their education. I am afraid that these morning sittings starting in June will have caused some setbacks to some of the boys, but I understand these boys do not intend to continue school in any event.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Health and Welfare
NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE 238. Departmental administration, $1,601,785.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I start out by suggesting that it would be very kind of opposition members if they were to treat me as kindly as they did Mr. Speaker. Of course, that is probably a little too much to expect. I have a statement, Mr. Chairman, and if hon. members so desire I would be glad to make it on the opening item of the department. I might point out that actually I propose to make a further statement on civil defence when we come to that item. I am in the hands of the committee. If, due to the special situation that seems to prevail today, hon. members do not necessarily wish me to make any remarks on the opening item of this department, I would be pleased to forgo them.
I believe the minister has not got a very long statement, and this is a rather important department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You should know.
As the minister says, I should know. I think the expenditures involved are so large and so many important matters are involved that some statement should be made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
As hon. members will note from the blue book, we are budgeting for an expenditure of $1,393,340,528 for the 12-month period ending March 31, 1960. An additional amount of $7,220,817 is provided for civil defence purposes.
Of our over-all expected outlay of roughly $1.4 billion, 94 per cent covers statutory items including $577.6 million to be expended from the old age security fund. Only 6 per cent or $92 million represents items to be voted by parliament.
While our total estimates embody an increase of over $220 million as compared with the past fiscal year, non-statutory items show a decrease for the first time in eight years. Amounting to $1.3 million, this decrease relates chiefly to a reduction in estimated expenditures under the national health grants. I want to emphasize that there has been no reduction-nor is any contemplated-in the funds available to the provinces through the grants. The lower estimate simply represents an appraisal of actual provincial needs during the fiscal year.
The largest increase in expenditures arises from a new statutory item in our estimates, that is, federal payments under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. Running to $160 million, this item represents 72.7 per cent of the total increase in statutory outlays. Other increases in statutory items
6340	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare include: $25 million for family allowances, related primarily to population growth; $22,600,000 for old age security pensions, reflecting the growing number of persons 70 years of age and over; $2,700,000, $2,200,000 and $300,000 for old age assistance, disabled persons allowances and blind persons allowances respectively, reflecting the anticipated increase in persons eligible for benefits under these programs; $8,960,000 for unemployment assistance, related largely to the effects of the removal of the threshold governing federal sharing under this program.
In addition to giving this general outline of our proposed expenditures for the present fiscal year, I might touch on a number of aspects of the department's operations which strike me as particularly significant.
On the health side, there is the hospital insurance plan which has now completed its first full year of operation in five provinces. I know that hon. members will be pleased to learn that this important and complex project is working out extremely well. While certain problems have been encountered, the over-all picture has been one of smooth and orderly development. In fact, as I told the recent biennial meeting of the Canadian Hospital Association, I think it is fair to say that the program has come through its immediate post-natal period with flying colours.
To my mind, what has been achieved in this matter reflects great credit on Canada's health team. In particular I would mention the excellent co-operation that has been extended to us at the federal level by provincial ministers and their officials. This has been a key element in the successful launching of what is probably the most ambitious and far-reaching health measure ever undertaken in Canada.
At the moment, the hospital insurance program covers nearly 12 million Canadians in eight provinces, New Brunswick's plan having commenced on July 1. As I have already announced to the house, we are also ready to sign an agreement with Prince Edward Island but, at its request, this has been put off until July 20. The plan itself is scheduled to go into effect on October 1. In addition, preparations are going ahead in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and both hope to have plans under way early in 1960.
With respect to costs, I am encouraged by the fact that these have been running about as expected. While final calculations of federal payments for 1958-59 have yet to be made, the pattern of our monthly advances to the provinces has been most favourable, corresponding in large degree to prior estimates. As of March 31, federal advances totalled
IMr. Monteith (Perth).]

nearly $55 million as against the estimated figure of $60 million for 1958-59 which appears in the blue book. Since these advances were based on preliminary returns from the provinces, it is likely that final payments will be even closer to our forecast.
Continued progress has also been made in another important federal-provincial health measure. Now in its fourth year of operation, the Salk polio vaccine program has provided protection to nearly 7 million Canadians, both children and adults. Among those covered recently are many members of this house, of the other place, and of the parliamentary staff. In this connection, I should like to express a word of thanks to the doctors in the house for their initiative' in setting up and carrying out their own immunization program. My department has, of course, been only too happy to supply the vaccine for this purpose, and I understand that over 900 inoculations have so far been administered.
Turning to the welfare side of the department's operations, the outstanding highlight of the past year was, of course, the completion of the Clark report on "Economic Security for the Aged in the United States and Canada". I am sure all hon. members will agree that it represents a most comprehensive study of the subject. As far as the government is concerned, we consider that Dr. Clark has carried out a very difficult assignment with great distinction, and are gratified at the favourable reception which has been accorded the report throughout the country. At this stage, I can only say that it is being studied closely by the government.
Another development of note is the entry of the province of Quebec into the unemployment assistance program which I announced to the house earlier this month. Under an agreement signed on July 1, Quebec becomes the tenth province to participate in this important social welfare measure. Unemployment assistance has proved of great value in other parts of the country and the dominion government is naturally pleased that the people of Quebec will now be in a position to share in its benefits.
Since this event occurred subsequent to the preparation and tabling of our estimates for the current fiscal period, it may be expected that federal unemployment assistance payments to all ten provinces-including Quebec -will be somewhat in excess of the $20,960,000 figure shown for 1959-60 in the blue book.
I mentioned earlier that I proposed to make a statement on civil defence when the item comes up for consideration.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to express my sincere thanks to the officers and

staff of the department. With the passage of time, I am increasingly mindful of what their skill and dedication to duty mean to our very extensive operations.

Mr. Chairman, the minister concluded his statement by paying a tribute and expressing his gratitude to the officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I should like to join him-not that I have any right to do it at the present time except for their collaboration during the period when I was their minister-knowing them as I do, in a tribute to a remarkable group of pubic servants who have made a great contribution in this department both on the health and on the welfare side, and as well as in civil defence.
The minister has suggested that as we were kind to the Speaker who preceded him in the discussion of the latter's estimates-I refer to the discussion of the Speaker's estimates- that he would hope that he would get similar treatment. I can assure the minister that there is no necessary contradiction between kindness and constructive criticism. He can be assured that he will be treated in any event with great fairness.
I want to say to the minister something which I would have said last year if I had been here for the discussion of the estimates of this department, and that is that, as the former minister, I appreciated and I continue to greatly appreciate what I understand from all sides is the generous and fair way in which the minister has treated members of the department, particularly those in my own office.
The minister proposes to make a statement when we come to the civil defence item, and of course I cannot say anything about that at this time except generally to comment on one or two matters which I believe should receive attention. As the minister has pointed out, most of the expenditures in the Department of National Health and Welfare are of an uncontrollable type; that is to say, they are either statutory or they involve services in connection with which there could be no governmental or ministerial interference, certainly in the latter case without causing the greatest hardship and dislocation. In respect of the non-statutory items totalling something in the neighbourhood, I think the minister said, of $92 million, the decrease which he called our attention to arises out of a decrease of around $1 million in the national health grants. This decrease in turn was because the provinces, either collectively or individually, did not require certain assistance which theoretically is open to them under the national health grants vote. The minister has given us the assurance that this
Supply-Health and Welfare did not in any way mean an impairment of the assistance parliament has authorized the federal government to give the provinces to supplement their efforts to maintain the excellent health services which prevail in all of our provinces in varying degrees.
I would be very interested when we come to the particular item to learn exactly in what grant the decrease has taken place. Likewise when we come to that item the minister could possibly give us a more detailed picture of the operation of the health grants which, as he knows, were established, among other reasons, for the purpose of laying down a very necessary foundation for the system of hospital insurance that has now been so successfully undertaken in this country. I am sure the minister with two years of experience now will agree that these grants have greatly assisted the provinces in carrying out work in the field of public health, work that could not fully have been discharged by them but for the assistance that was given to them by the government of the day some 11 or 12 years ago. These grants, which as I say were not necessarily conditional on the establishment of hospital insurance, were a necessary prerequisite to the setting up on a basis of co-operation with the provinces a system of hospital insurance that has now been undertaken so successfully in Canada.
The minister mentioned the Salk polio vaccine of which some 7 million Canadians have now been recipients and who are enjoying the advantage of the discovery of Dr. Salk. If it had not been for the national health program, for the moneys which were available at the will of the federal government, this program would certainly not have been as successful in Canada, and many of the provinces would undoubtedly not have been able to take advantage of the arrangements which were made at the time by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The minister has mentioned that the beneficiaries of this Salk vaccine program are not confined to young children, but that adults may benefit as well. I would be interested at some time during the estimates to know exactly to what extent the federal government participates in the administration of the Salk polio vaccine to adults, and whether the financial sharing formula is the same as prevailed two years ago with respect to young children.
The minister has a research grant under the national health program, and that research grant was able to play its part in the development by Dr. Salk himself of the Salk polio vaccine. I was interested the other night when the estimates of the national


the report be prepared as early as possible so that parliament and the public could judge whether or not anything further could be done in this field. Nothing is going to be done this session. I am sure that nothing will be done next session. I have great doubts whether it will be done the following session, but I would not be surprised-and perhaps the minister can give us some assurances on this particular-that on the eve of the next election, realizing how-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Such as hospital insurance in 1957.

The minister says "such as hospital insurance in 1957". Hospital insurance was not a pre-election pledge. My hon. friend now has the documents and he knows that hospital insurance introduced by the former government represented hard work on the part of all concerned, provincial and federal officials, and ministers. It represented a sincere desire; it was not a pre-election pledge, and certainly it was never offered in the way in which this United States program was offered.
I say to the minister, a lot of money was spent in the preparation of the Clark report. If there are any advantages to the United States system, this government has the moral responsibility to take steps at the earliest moment to implement the promise made by the Prime Minister. If he does not, this will be one other promise made to capture the support of the Canadian people, a promise made with all of the vigour and the freshness that attended so many other promises but, like all other promises, it will be a promise unfulfilled.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the spirit of the committee and on such a day as this I am going to make my normally brief comments even briefer than usual today.
I should like first of all to compliment the hon. member who has just taken his seat on two or three matters on which he spoke. I wholeheartedly concur with him in some of these matters and the fact that he has presented his views so clearly today will certainly save me the necessity of repeating them.
Sometimes there is a bit of confusion caused by the two hon. members of the same name. In view of his past distinguished service and of his present very comprehensive criticism of this subject, I might better refer to him as "Doctor" Martin and we can get away from some of the confusion that exists.
Some refer to me as Farmer Martin.
We all have to have our little joke.

I should like to compliment him first on the way in which he presented his case in regard to the great need in this country for and the justifiable expectations of some sort of pension plan similar to what they have in the United States at the present time. I should like to concur in his remarks along that line. I am sure that many of the Canadian people have looked forward to this. I have had the opportunity of travelling across the country from coast to coast in the last couple of years and in many parts of the country I have met with a very strong wish on the part of Canadians that some action will be taken in this field.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that it is far too important a field to be left to just prior to the next election. We have had too much of that in the past. For many years health insurance was promised to the people of Canada. I hope this is one practice that the present government will not pick up from the previous one.
I think, Mr. Chairman, I will confine my comments today to a few remarks about the nospital insurance plan. I should like to stress this particular aspect of it. After a wait of 40 years for the implementation of hospital insurance as the first step toward health insurance in this country, the fact that within one year all the provinces but one have adopted hospital insurance after the federal government took the lead is an excellent example of the need for federal leadership in matters of this kind. The hon. member for Essex East referred to that very point, that the results at the end of one year of the plan show that the many fears that were expressed were in fact groundless. I cannot resist the opportunity to point out that that is exactly what members of this party have said for many, many years. These fears have been demonstrated to be groundless in many other parts of the world and I think that the sooner we proceed the sooner we will find that fears with regard to complete health insurance have no more basis in fact than those expressed with regard to hospital insurance.
I think the federal government should also take the lead in co-operation with the provinces to iron out some of the possible difficulties that may arise from time to time in the implementation of the provincial hospital plans. In the government's position as a sort of co-ordinator for all the provinces I think they can be of terrific assistance in advising the provinces as to what problems may come up from time to time. If the federal government takes the lead in this field I think they
Supply-Health and Welfare can be of considerable assistance to the provinces in carrying out their plans. I think this also points up the need of federal leadership because provincial leadership in this field is definitely not enough.
In the last 14 or 15 years we have had an example of a provincial hospital insurance plan which paved the way toward hospital insurance generally. I think it is very significant that many people whom I have met who have had considerable criticism for other aspects of the Saskatchewan government have been practically universal in their agreement that Saskatchewan today has the best hospital insurance plan in the country. They will also agree that through the implementation of the hospital insurance plan the province of Saskatchewan also enjoys the best hospitals on a per capita basis of any province in this country. I think this is a natural thing that will follow the implementation of hospital insurance.
Before the minister's estimates are finished I should like him to give some indication of when we can expect tuberculosis, mental illnesses and so forth to be included under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. I think he will recall the great number of times that members of the present cabinet have advocated this in the house.
There is one other point I should like to recall to the minister and that is the fact that almost two years have passed since the last increase was made in old age pensions. I think he will also recall that at that time a very definite commitment was made to the old age pensioners that this was merely a temporary matter and that as soon as things got straightened away further consideration was going to be given to this need. I think he will also realize that in these two years the cost of living has crept up considerably and that the need is far greater now than it was when this promise was made to the Canadian people.
In addition, I hope that the department has under consideration the necessary steps to adjust the age limits downward in the face of the situation we have today of more and more people once they reach the age of 50 finding themselves in very difficult circumstances. With the advances in technology, with automation and all the dislocations it causes we have an ever-increasing number of Canadians reaching the age of 60 to 65, being thrown out of employment through no fault of their own and finding it practically impossible to obtain new employment because of their age. One thing that could help this category of people would be the early implementation of a social security plan based on that of the United States because I firmly

Supply-Health and Welfare believe that one of the major reasons why-people in this age group are finding it so difficult to obtain employment is the fact that industrial pension plans throughout the country, all in the hands of various private insurance companies, contain clauses barring people after a certain age. That points out all the more clearly the need for the federal government to take the lead in this field.
In view of the circumstances I think that is all I will deal with today. I should like to add once more that I hope the minister will show the zeal in his department that has been shown by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and I hope he will show the industry in his department that has been shown by the Minister of Public Works. This is one of the most important fields of activity in the whole country and I hope that the minister and his department will take the necessary lead.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister and the government on doing something in connection with civil defence. This is a matter in which I am really interested.

speechtext: Would the hon. member mind making his remarks on the civil defence item which will come up a little later?
I now have the floor and I am afraid that if I sit down and give it to someone else I will not have a chance again. In any event I will be very brief.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: All right.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would advise the hon. member that it was agreed that when we came to item 351 there would be a full discussion of civil defence. Perhaps the hon. member might wish to wait until then?
Yes.

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to touch on the effects of lower and marginal radiation doses. A little less than two years ago the minister announced that some research work was being done by the department into the genetic effects of marginal radiation on humans. I should like to hear his report on that today, and also whether he has any results to report as to the detection of strontium 90 in milk and cereals. Apart from the health effects, I think a fallout of strontium 90 in western Canada could have very bad economic effects for our western farmers. I do not intend to say any more on radiation but I should like the minister to make a report after I am finished.
I should like to refer now to a subject which seems to be contentious in different parts of our country, the fluoridation of water.


The salts of fluorine called fluorides are natural constituents of practically all our *water supplies. It is never a matter of whether or not the water contains fluorine, it is always a question of whether or not it contains enough. In early childhood it is necessary to have a sufficient intake of the fluorides to make a good hard dentine formation and the good teeth that should be developed.
There is a difference of opinion amongst members of the medical and dental profession as to the quantity of fluorine required to produce a good, hard enamel. It is generally agreed, however, that drinking water should contain not less than one part per million of fluorine in order to obtain this objective. The water of many of our wells in Canada contains considerably more than one part per million, and often as much as two or three parts per million, while the water in the great lakes system from which many of our population centres obtain their water supply contains very much less than one part per million. The point is that caries of the teeth is very prevalent in children who drink water where their source of water supply is the great lakes system and where the fluorine content is lower.
This was very vividly brought home to me some years ago. In my part of the country there is a graded school in which about one-half of the students come from the country and the other half come from an area that is supplied by the Welland water works, and Welland gets its water from the Welland canal shortly after it leaves lake Erie. It was interesting, in examining the teeth of these children to find that those coming from the area supplied by the Welland water works had an incidence of caries practically 70 per cent greater than those who came from the country in which their drinking water was taken from wells where the supply of fluorine was ample.
Caries of the teeth is serious. It is one of the most common chronic diseases. I think it is probably the most common. It has its economic aspects, namely the cost of filling the teeth, which is never satisfactory, and in addition if the enamel is soft we know that the teeth continue to decay and dentures will be required. Then too, the abscess formations which result from caries of the teeth do start many of the degenerating processes in the body to which man is heir. I have seen many conditions such as heart conditions, high blood pressure and joint conditions resembling rheumatism and peripheral pain largely clear up after the removal of infected teeth. Many of these infected teeth have been carried for years and, no

doubt, add to chronic ill health and the development of chronic conditions in vital organs which tend to shorten life.
Several municipalities in Ontario have fluoridation. I believe Brantford was the first and I am glad to say that my home town was the second. It was started in my home town in 1952 and already the decrease in the incidence of caries of teeth in children has been cut down by 70 per cent. Unfortunately, in Ontario at the present time, if a municipality votes to have the domestic water fluoridated, it is not allowed by the government of Ontario. In those municipalities already adding fluorine to the water, a few citizens just have to apply to the municipal council and the council is then obliged to submit the question to a vote.
Prior to the vote all kinds of subterfuges are used by the anti-fluoridationists. They put up signs, for example, around the town saying that the water supply is not pure, that it contains rat poison and what not. This has quite an effect on different people living in the town, and particularly those catering to the tourist industry.
In my town, for example, we have been through this and I know that it cost the dentists and physicians in the town money to carry on the campaign. The people voted to continue using fluorine in the water, but I think the question can be brought up again next year if enough people apply to the town. One very important thing was said to me at the time of that vote, and that was that the national health minister had never made a pronouncement on fluorine. Practically all our large universities accept fluorine as being very necessary to prevent caries of the teeth. It is highly endorsed by practically all the American public health associations; the American dental association, the American medical association, and their counterparts in Canada.
The world health organization in Geneva highly recommended fluoridation and Canada, among many other countries, accepted the principle of fluoridation. I realize that matters relating to health come directly under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but this is a matter in which I think our Minister of National Health and Welfare should give leadership. On the occasion of the visit of Her Majesty to Ottawa the Prime Minister announced the establishment of a fund of $1 million for research into the diseases of children. With this I agreed, but it occurred to me how much misery and disease in children the government might prevent by merely spreading knowledge of the techniques already known but not publicized.
I have looked over the press very carefully and can find only one reference the minister
Supply-Health and Welfare ever made to fluoridation. This is contained in a letter written to and published by Mr. William R. Fulton, director of civic affairs, Calgary junior chamber of commerce, in the Calgary Herald of September 30, 1957. I have a copy of this letter here, and I will paraphrase it. The minister goes on to say that he thinks fluoridation is an important landmark in the long quest for control of tooth decay; that tooth decay is an incurable disease and the only real hope lies in its prevention; that fluorine in the amount of 1 to 1.2 parts per million parts of water is harmless and will cut down tooth decay by at least 60 per cent. This is an important matter to the health of the people who drink this water. If the minister believes what he wrote in September, 1957, and I think what he wrote is very strong, why has he kept so quiet about it for a whole year and a half? After all, that statement was put in the press by somebody else to whom the minister had written a letter.
I do not think any member of this house would say that health matters should be political, and yet it seems to me that the minister considers it to be so. Premier Frost of Ontario has not taken any stand on fluoridation except to appoint a commission to inquire into it. The department of health in Ottawa is the senior department in Canada, is a member of the world health organization and has all the very latest information available to it from this world-wide organization. I think Canadians have the right to expect direction from the minister of health. As I said, he has made no official announcement on fluorine, and I hope that it is not because this has not suited Premier Frost politically. I do not think the minister should ever be subservient to any provincial premier in so far as the health of the people is concerned, I would certainly appeal to him to make some pronouncement. Certainly, he has a duty to help our children in Canada, particularly our children living near the great lakes who have a very high incidence of caries of the teeth.

Mr. Chairman, the best asset that this country has is not the gold in the ground nor the wheat in the bins but it is the people who inherit this fair land of ours. If we see to it that they have informed minds and healthy bodies, tempered with a reasonable amount of religious instruction, I do not think we shall have to worry about the destiny of Canada.
I think it was with this thought of a healthy body in mind that prompted the hon. member for Simcoe East together with other hon. members of this house to follow the medical profession to band together in a house health
6348	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare league to minister to the needs of the other members of this house and staff. I think we would be very remiss in our duties if we did not record our appreciation to these gentlemen, assisted by the efficient nurse on the house staff, for their untiring and great effort on our behalf. I feel that I am not only expressing my own feelings in this regard but those of all the other hon. members of the house.

It appears to me that the tendency and effort today is to confine remarks, and to make them brief, something, which is of course easy for me to do and to deal on the first item of particular estimates. While some comments I may have to make will relate to specific items I hope that I may be able to get them in on this first item and that we can rattle through the rest in a sort of machine gun fashion as has been the practice today anyway.
Following the question which I asked of the minister a few days ago I should like to make a few comments about the use and the extremely harmful effects arising from the use of these polyethylene plastic bags that are used quite extensively in the dry cleaning field as covers for clothes and which I understand range in thickness to something less than thousandths of an inch. From reading the newspapers from time to time we all know that these bags unfortunately have caused the death of a number of children both here and in the United States. I have seen the figures of children having been smothered by these polyethylene bags. I have also seen the figures as of the day before yesterday, when another account was given of the death of a child arising out of the same circumstances. Sixty children have suffocated from their use. It is extremely unfortunate that the developers or manufacturers of these particular bags or this particular type of plastic being used for this purpose were not able to foresee the possible detrimental effect they would have. I also read that the industry itself is contemplating a widespread agitational and publicity campaign to bring to the attention of the public, and particularly to that of mothers who have small children, the danger that may result or the harm that could come from the injudicious use of these particular plastic bags.
In this regard I think the Department of National Health and Welfare, not only in so far as polyethylene bags are concerned but as to other items of a similar nature which might be injurious to the health of our people or endanger their lives, should be in a position to take some corrective measures in so far as the use of these bags is concerned. As I understand the situation now,


about the extent of the activity of the department in so far as statutory authority is concerned, as was expressed by the minister in answer to my question, was notably one of publicity and hoping to draw to the attention of everybody in the country to be extremely careful in the use of these bags. It is extremely unfortunate that 40, 50 or 60 children-whatever the number is-or even one child should have suffered loss of life because of the use of things such as these. Even if it is necessary to get some broad general powers of inspection or regulation in so far as these items are concerned, I hope the minister will undertake to confer with the justice department and with his own officials in order to see whether in the future the department cannot go more into the field of regulation rather than in the field of publicity after the damage has been done. I hope that even now, with the publicity campaign that I understand is being carried on by the people in the industry itself, will have some effect and that parents of small children will realize the danger that exists in using these bags and allowing them to get into the hands of children. I hope they will take steps to destroy them as soon as they are able to take them off whatever article they cover.
I should also like to mention a few references and comments with regard to the drug industry and the relation between administrators in the food and drugs division and the manufacturers and distributors of the various pharmaceuticals and second with regard to what I consider in many cases to be the unnecessarily high cost of drugs. I believe anyone who has had occasion to have a prescription given to him by a doctor and then has taken that prescription to a pharmacist will agree with this statement. In most cases people have been shocked by the high costs which they may have to pay for certain drugs which are necessary for ailments they may have. It is not uncommon for people to find charges of $10, $15 or $20 for one prescription. This is quite a shock to the patient. In many cases people find themselves in an extremely embarrassing position in not being able to afford to pay that kind of money for some particular drug that is prescribed for them.
I discussed this question with a couple of friends of mine who are medical practitioners. They say that they have not kept track of statistics but they recall a number of occasions on which, when they have prescribed something, the patient has asked them how much it will cost; and that when they gave an estimate of the cost the patient has then said, "Can you not prescribe something cheaper?" An independent survey was made

in the city of Toronto. How factual these figures are I could not say. However, it has been indicated to me by a person in the pharmaceutical field that upwards of 30 per cent of the prescriptions written by physicians are not filled because of the high prices. People will go into the drug store and inquire as to the price of the prescription, find that it is unnecessarily high and then say "I do not feel quite that ill; perhaps I will hold off for a while, I just have not the money at the moment". Consequently they do not get the prescription filled and they do not get the drugs which may be of some help and benefit to them.
As to high costs, especially in connection with newly introduced drugs, the argument is used that it is necessary for the manufacturer in the first few months or years of sale and distribution of the drug to attempt to recapture his research costs as quickly as possible because with the advent of new drugs replacing old ones and new names replacing old brand names and so on, he may find that the drug on which he has spent money in connection with research in order to develop it fails with the public because something new has come along. This may be a commendable attitude for the drug manufacturer to take and in keeping with our present understanding of business practices, which operate on a profit. However, I am of the opinion that the prices of some drugs are maintained at an arbitrarily high level long after the research costs have been recaptured by the manufacturer.
There is a group of drugs generally referred to as tetracyclines. The percentage of prescriptions which are written for the tetracycline drugs is a matter of speculation, but I have been told that the United States pharmaceutical industry has estimated that 25 per cent of the total volume of drug sales in the United States involve tetracyclines. So far as Canada is concerned there are five companies who produce and distribute the tetracyclines under different brand names. The five companies are: Leclcrle Laboratories, Bristol Laboratories, Pfizer of Canada, E. R. Squibb and Sons and Upjohn Company of Canada. These five companies, because of the uniformity of price and because this price level has been high ever since their introduction on the market, are responsible for some sort of price conspiracy to maintain an arbitrarily high price level. I appreciate that is a question which can be dealt with more appropriately by the combines investigation branch, but I mention it because it is involved in the entire question of drugs.
So far as these brand names which are used by the various companies manufacturing
Supply-Health and Welfare tetracyclines are concerned, this is an indication of the price structure. The price for the manufacture of 16 capsules is uniformly $5.66, and the suggested retail price is $9.44, which represents a 66 per cent difference. I raise this question for two reasons. One is because, as I mentioned earlier, of the total volume of sales of these drugs as indicated by the pharmaceutical industry in the United States; secondly, this particular antibiotic covers a fairly wide range of use and extends to the treatment of quite a large number of ailments. I am sure that any of the hon. members of the house who are medical practitioners would be able to go into more complete detail about the effective use of the various tetracyclines themselves and the type of ailments which they treat.
I would also suggest that there is an arbitrarily high price maintained so far as penicillin is concerned. That is a drug which has also been on the market for quite a number of years. However, as I said that is a question for the combines investigation branch and I only mention it in passing because of its relationship to the administrators of the food and drug division and the industry itself, both the manufacturing and distributing ends of it.
In recent years we have seen, probably in the United States more than in Canada, a pretty wide ranging and I think indiscriminate use of the so-called tranquillizers. Again the United States pharmaceutical industry estimates that the prescription sales which apply to tranquillizers run somewhere in the neighbourhood of 25 per cent. Here in Canada I do not know what the across the counter sales are without prescription, but I have been told that tranquillizers like most other drugs have side effects which were not envisaged when the drug was originally developed. Further, the side effects may develop after a period of use which may change with the individual.
While tranquillizers have been used to quite a great extent in psychiatric work and treatment in mental hospitals, it has been noted with people who use these tranquillizers that they do develop side effects resulting from this use. Some patients might be diagnosed incorrectly by a physician and treated for an ailment which he does not have, and of course that could have very serious consequences to the patient. I am not in any way casting reflections upon the medical profession for not being able properly to diagnose a patient's ailments, but these are opinions expressed by people who have used the drugs, and they have used the classic case of Parkinson's disease, where the continued use of tranquillizers might result

Supply-Health and Welfare in what is called pseudo-Parkinsonism. As one might imagine, that is not a very happy ailment for one to have, and if it is not diagnosed correctly a person may carry on with the indiscriminate use of tranquillizers and find himself in an unfortunate position.
I think as far as this department is concerned steps should be immediately taken so that tranquillizers may be sold only on prescription under the direction of a doctor who is able to regulate the use of the drug and make sure the patient does not get it indiscriminately and possibly develop all sorts of other side effects.
I was going to make some comments about dispensing fees of pharmacists. This is a factor to a degree in the high cost of drugs. To what extent it is a factor it is not possible to say unless one could get hold of a list of dispensing fees established by the various colleges of pharmacy which exist in the country. In many cases the sole function of the pharmacist is just to read the doctor's handwriting and pick up the correct bottle off the shelf and give it to the customer. It does not require now the same degree of proficiency as was required of pharmacists many years ago when they had to mix their own drugs to the prescription of the doctor. This is a field which could bear some investigation.
I am told also that as far as the purchase of drugs is concerned by various governmental departments, there should be a closer check. I suggest that so far as we are able to discover at the moment the Department of Defence Production in its purchases of drugs for the armed forces apparently concentrates on the lowest price quoted for a particular drug. This in terms of quality of drugs could result, and does result in some cases, in the armed forces having purchased for them and having dispensed to them drugs which may be of an inferior quality. I would suggest in this regard that through our own drugs division we might be able to get in touch and establish some liaison with the Department of Defence Production in an attempt to see whether that department will purchase these drugs under the same regulatory control as the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am not suggesting that the drugs are inferior or produced under unclean conditions but some appear not to be produced with the care that goes into the production of others.
Because this is a complex question affecting many, and inasmuch as this is the era of royal commissions which this government delights in appointing, I would suggest that a royal commission be established to deal


with the whole field of drugs and pharmaceuticals inquiring into all aspects of research and production and the impact of competition. In other words, the terms of reference should be as broad as possible. I would suggest the appointment to the commission of a highly competent medical practitioner, a pharmacologist, an economist, a lawyer with extensive knowledge in the combines field and a psychiatrist because all these factors are involved in the question.
There are many other subjects one could discuss at this time but they have been dealt with to some extent by those hon. members who have participated in the debate up to this point. In my view the health and welfare of the Canadian people are of prime importance, our most important resource. Every effort should be bent toward preserving, and enhancing the health and welfare of our citizens. Inasmuch as this department is subsidized I hope it will not be accorded the same treatment given to a branch of another department about which we heard today and which some hon. members claimed was subsidized and therefore should be interfered with.

Mr. Chairman, I trust that I will not prove to be a tranquillizer for those on the front benches. I shall be penurious with time and keep my promise in making my remarks as brief as possible. I had prepared a first class speech on the subject but the committee will be denied it in the closing days of the session.
There is a growing concern in Canada, the United States and other countries about fallout. This was the subject of an interesting debate in the British House of Commons recently. I intended to deal with this at some greater length but I shall now leave it for a later occasion.
There is a growing concern in Canada and other countries about a lack of information on the question of fallout and an increasing suspicion that the public are not being told all the facts with respect to the question. From periodicals I have read I know there is a feeling in the United States that the defence department of that country is having some effect on the public being given the information they are seeking in this connection.
To make my remarks brief I shall quote from an article in the July 5, 1959, issue of The Reporter entitled "A Primer on Fallout" which I commend to the attention of all who are interested in the question as being informative and authoritative:
The nation's press gave surprisingly meagre coverage to the second congressional fallout hearings that were held in Washington from May 5 to

May 8. The New York Times, for example, devoted only three inside-page stories to the testimony that was given before Representative Chet Holifield's special subcommittee on radiation of the joint congressional committee on atomic energy; a fourth story headlined "Study Minimizes Fallout Danger" (carried on page 1 and exceeding in length the other three combined) gave details of a reassuring report that was released during the hearings by the atomic energy commission's general advisory committee.
The coverage in most other papers was even poorer than that in the Times. One noteworthy exception, the New York Daily News, carried a concise two-part roundup of the hearings several days after they ended instead of attempting to cover them as "spot news". But in general the press has all but ignored the most complete summary of the fallout situation currently available.
The same applies to the press of Canada with respect to these most important findings and hearings. Another section of the article reads:
Dr. Arthur H. Wolff of the PHS commented on this point as follows:
I think we are generally agreed that strontium-90 as an environmental contaminant certainly deserves the primary attention, because the problem will persist for many years following the cessation of nuclear weapons testing. But I think data collected during the past few years does indicate that some of the shorter-lived isotopes, particularly iodine-131, are not necessarily insignificant-
It is particularly important to look in the young age group . . . Much of the work that has been done in the past has been with adults-
I trust the minister will deal with the question when replying to our remarks because it is important to present and future generations. The people of Canada, the United States and other nations are demanding the truth and the facts with respect to this problem and I trust this government will give the facts to the Canadian people as they are obtained.

Let me assure him that I am not. However, he also mentioned radiation. I would say that studies have been carried out in conjunction with the national research council to determine the genetically significant dose to the general population resulting from the medical use of X-rays. When tabling the report on radiation recently I spoke in the house.
I could say considerably more if required. We are giving it very serious study. We are setting up a total body monitoring unit which will be in use before very long. In the report I tabled some time ago, and in my remarks accompanying the tabling of that report, I pointed out that we are increasing our testing for radiation purposes. I think I can say no more than that we are completely aware of and are examining very carefully the effects of radiation. While I feel that there is no need to panic in respect of this particular matter, we certainly have not lost sight of the fact that it does require very close examination.
The hon. member for Kootenay West was interested in this particular subject and I am sorry that time did not allow him to continue to discuss what had transpired in the British House of Commons. I appreciated the fact that he had discussed this personally with me earlier.
The hon. member for Skeena certainly brought forward some thought-provoking matters for consideration. I quite agree with his thinking on the plastic bag matter. I thank him for bringing it to the attention of the committee today. I feel that, as I said the other day, at the moment the only way we can do very much in this respect is to bring it to public notice, and the fact that he has brought it up here today does contribute to bringing the dangers of this plastic


bag situation to public notice. I have also seen in the paper that the association themselves are taking steps to advertise the dangers of this particular article.
As far as the high price of drugs is concerned, I know they are expensive. I have bought a considerable amount in my lifetime. The hon. member himself mentioned that the companies must recover research and development expenses. I think he probably had the idea that maybe the companies continue to collect these development and research expenses longer than is necessarily required. I am not in a position to comment on that. I would suspect, however, that the combines people probably are examining any possibility of a combine in drug prices. I do not think I have anything further to say at the moment, except to agree with the hon. member for Skeena's closing remark that the health of our nation is probably its most important asset. It certainly will be my endeavour, as long as I am in this office, to keep that foremost in my mind.

I was called out for a few
minutes and I only heard the latter part of the minister's statement with respect to my suggestions and comments. I do not know whether he dealt in his earlier remarks with some of the things I said. I should like him to indicate his thoughts and ideas on the suggestion of the necessity of a royal commission in the drug field in order to ascertain many factors that are unknown at the moment with respect to whether these drug companies are continuing to recoup what they originally classify as research costs beyond a normal period of time and also whether or not there is waste and squandering in research and advertising in an attempt to promote some of the pharmaceuticals that are developed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I feel that I must not leave any doubt as to how I stand on this matter. I certainly would not suggest a royal commission in this respect. It think it is an inappropriate undertaking for a royal commission. The hon. member has intimated that some of these research and developments costs may be collected over a longer period of time than necessary. That may be so. I am not in a position to deny such a possibility but I cannot believe that is true of the over-all picture. While some of these drugs appear expensive, I have known of drugs to be particularly expensive when they first came on the market and shortly afterwards, when development and research costs had been partially collected, the drug gradually came down in price. I do not think I could justify the suggestion that a royal commission be appointed.

The minister referred to the question of the maintenance of high prices for an unnecessarily long period of time and said that drugs had appeared on the market at high prices and that the price had gradually declined as time went on. Has the minister looked at the matter sufficiently carefully to determine whether the decline in price took place because the product developed was not under patent and other drug manufacturers were able to enter the field, analyse the drug, alter it slightly and reproduce the same thing without becoming involved in research costs to the same extent? Would he be able to say whether it would not be a case of a drug being developed by one company and not being patented and another company entering the field and producing the same thing under another trade name at a lower price, a company which did not do any initial research but merely stole-maybe the industry would look at it that way-or purchased the drug, analysed it and developed a similar product without extensive research costs, thus by competition bringing down the price of the produce? Would that not be the ease rather than the company producing the drug having a patent and exclusive rights to market the product with the result that the cost of the product to the consumer would decline as time went on and research costs were recouped?

303. Preparatory work, not within the fields of particular departments, on emergency defence measures, $175,000.

Mr. Chairman, there was only one question raised and that had to do with the powers under the Defence Production Act. That question was asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and he pointed out that certain of the powers under the Defence Production Act were being allowed to lapse. May I point out that those powers will be lapsing at the end of July and are sections 23 to 31 of the Defence Production Act.
Those particular powers were extraordinary powers, and powers of unusual import. Section 23 provides that any person refusing a contract from the Minister of Defence Production may be ordered to comply, and that any person refusing to comply to a direction would be liable for the loss thereof and for damage thereto. Then section 24 provided that the minister might requisition supplies made by notice in writing, and direct any person who owns or has in his possession or control defence supplies, to have them requisitioned on behalf of Her Majesty. Section 27 says that where the minister is satisfied that a person who has entered into a defence contract has failed or is likely to fail to perform the contract in a businesslike and efficient manner, he may authorize another person to carry on.
Section 28 provides that the governor in council may, by order, direct that a person shall not be bound by any obligation, restriction or limitation imposed on that person by any statute, order, regulation or contract. In other words, these extraordinary powers provided rights and assured authority which was overwhelming in its import, to which of course, when we were in opposition, we took strong objection.
These extraordinary powers will lapse, as I said, at the end of this month because, as has already been pointed out, the government does not intend to continue in days of peace powers which, although properly exercisable in wartime, ought not to be used in days of peace. With regard to what I suggested last evening, I want to say that these powers set out under the Defence Production Act are, in the opinion of the government, not necessary in days of peace and it would be inexcusable to continue them on the statute books beyond the period of their actual existence under the statute.
